i0#r-pil-15 nun-yk-il, &c., the ng being euphonic (compare Pitta-
Pitta pakoolangooro, sect. 36).

= hook-boomerang belonging-to-me mud digs-up.

Other Boulia District songs are —

y£r-tX yer-tik e-ri-£e-ch&

=* grass-tops (make) bough-shed.

ttta-la-kS nem--p& ka-rfl-pul-te-a

= dog (and) slut are-jumping, Ac.

The first verse of the song gives the name to the particular corrobboree :
cf. the European's " Pater Noster, " Alphabet," &c. (sect. 199).

197. (j) Music of the Song. — Unfortunately the actual harmony of the music I
have not been able to decipher : to my unmusical ear the cadences seem always
identical, a sort of wail commencing with a sudden rise and ending with a slow
prolonged fall.

198. (k) Beating of the Time.— The audience squat upon the ground, usually
in rows (in the Boulia District) ranged one behind the other, like the seats in the
old form of theatre-pit. The men sit in front, the women and children behind,
while the dogs are scattered anywhere around. Occasionally the audience is divided
into two groups, side by side, one for each sex. Both sexes, as has been already
mentioned, carry on the singing and both beat time, the men alone doing this with
two boomerangs, one held in either hand, made to strike one another on the flat :
the women clap the open hand on to the crutch of the thighs, and thus produce a
loud reverberation (Fig. 293). In the Leichhardt-Selwyn and Cloncurry
Districts, the women, instead of striking their thighs, occasionally employ a sort
of drum or small pillow made of opossum skin, Ac, filled with feathers, rags,
Ac., upon which they bang with the flat of the open hands : in the Mitakoodi
language the name of this pillow is pi-ka~bur-ra. To tintinabulate with boomerangs is called, in the Pitta- Pitta, moolka-lo vmnka-linga — i.e., to sing with the
sticks ; the clapping of the/ hands, in the same language, is poor-pa-le. What
with the barking of the dogs, the clapping of the hands, the beating of the
boomerangs, the chanting of the song, and the stamping of the dancers — the
weird and uncanny appearance presented by the costumes and the different
attitudes only lit up by the intervening fire, all help to produce a scene which
requires an abler pen than mine to describe.

199. (l) The Holonga Set of Corrobborees. — An account of this dance, together
with the stage directions as far as they could be followed and understood, may not
prove uninteresting here as indicative of the powers of memory that are exercised
in reciting a song the delivery of which takes upwards of five nights for its
completion. Here and there I will show how slight the variations are that may
occur over the distance of ninety miles which separate Glenormiston from Boulia :
the wonder is increased when it is remembered that the words are sung in a
language of which the singers of both localities are entirely ignorant. This same
corrobboree also draws into prominence the various changes of costumes throughout,

and the introduction of certain salient features which distinguish the " boss " or
" leader of the dance " . from the others : remaining points of interest are the
introduction of various implements only to be subsequently destroyed, and the
different attitudes assumed by the trunk and limbs.

The place of origin and peregrinations of this particular corrobboree, as far as
they could be traced, have been already referred to in sect. 191.

The meaning of the word Molonga (cf. Pitta-Pitta mo-ma) is difficult to

interpret in European fashion. It hardly corresponds with our conception of the

" devil," and yet at the same time it does signify an evil-doer from whom mischief

may be expected. He is invisible to ordinary mortals unless it be to the "doctors,""

The excitement having subsided on his\ndinal disappearance, the singing proceeds with —\n\nfcoo-too-la pa-ren-ja-r£tt-ja\nMfl-ti-en po-Zoo-loo w6l-lum-poo-#ia-ra\nka-r(2 \\)a.-td'\\*&~td la-pa-rmg-Xr^-ra.\nwin-na-wa-ra prin-j6l-/?0r-6n-jo.\n\nSinging is again kept up all night, but on this particular evening a sort of\npremium or reward in the shape of extra food, &c, is held out as a bait to keep\nthe men up and singing, the one who holds out till sunrise winning it. At sunrise\nthe whole series of performances is brought to a close by one performer (Fig. 308)\ndancing \"kurra putya,\" &c. (as at the second morning's entertainment), but\ninstead of the leafy bushes he holds an oval -shaped fiat piece of wood in his hands,\nwhich he sways from side to side. This implement, which is covered with featherdown on both sides, according to pattern, is intended to depict the female\ngenitals.\n\nThe dance being now completed, the women and children retire while the\nmoyerjo, together with the head-dresses, forked and other sticks that have been\nused during the preceding five nights, &c, are all consumed by fire. The sun is\nwell up over the horizon now.\n\n200. Fables, Tales, and Legends.— How far the following fables are traditional\nit is impossible to say. The women, and those men who are lazy, that is, who are\nalways loafing around the camp, are the best hands at telling them : a man in the\nfull vigour of mental and bodily physique looks upon it as womanish and childish,\nalmost derogatory, to know anything concerning them, and will almost invariably\nrefer to his gin when any such matters are inquired of. The large majority of\nthe stories refer to animals with human attributes, and in this connection it is\nwell to remember the traditional superstition throughout all these districts, of\nthose extremely remote times when all the birds and quadrupeds were blackfellows\n(sect. 39) : furthermore there is almost invariably some attempt made at explaining\nany physical peculiarity or conformation. The following tales were obtained all\nin the Boulia District : —\n\n201. (a) The Water-hen and the Emu. — An emu was hatching her eggs in\nclose proximity to a small water-hen, who was also engaged in the same interesting\noccupation. By-and-by both birds proceeded to walk along the grass for something to eat, and in the evening returned to their respective nests. The same\nthing happened next day. But on the following morning, the water-hen got up\nsomewhat earlier than usual and went her way. The emu happening to see her\nneighbour's eggs, said, \" Hullo ! big-fellow eggs all same like mine, me take him,\"\nand shifting from her own nest, sat upon them. As the afternoon drew on, the\nwater-hen returned home, and when she saw the emu appropriating her eggs,\nbegan growling, but being so much smaller a bird could not use force to turn her\naway. So she built a large fire, and threw all the ashes over her opponent, who\nthus got all her feathers browned : in retaliation, the emu threw her antagonist\ninto the flames, and burnt her legs for her, which resulted in their turning red.\n\n202. (b) The Galah-parrot and the Lizard. — One time, there was a row between\nthe galah and the lizard. The lizard took up a chisel (sect. 149) with which he cut\nthe bird upon the head, the result being that his \" top-knot \" jumped up like a\nwood-shaving, and the blood streaked down over his neck and breast (the red\n\n126 BECBXATION: COBBOBBOBEES, 8POBTS, AND GAMES.\n\nmark) : the galah, however, revenged himself by getting a lot of the \" prickly\nbendii \" or \"burr,\" and sticking it all ever the lizard's back, bo as to form the\nwarty growths there."
}

((*) The Two Fishermen.— Two blackfellows, a Yunda and a Pitta-Pitta,\nhaving made some nets went fishing in the Booloo-Booloo water-hole [on the \" 15-\nMile Creek\" branch of the Hamilton Eiver, where the Winton road crosses it, about\n15 miles from Bouiia, sect. 226]. By-and-by, Mul-ka-ri (sect. 260) said to them,\n\" You go along other fellow water-hole. Me want him this one water-hole myself.\"\nSo they turned round and made tracks for Parapijori [= Parapituri Water-hole on\nthe G-eorgina River — sect. 226), and as they were drawing near their destination\nsaw a lot of hawks flying about (sect. 225) : thus they knew that some one was\nalready camped there. Nevertheless, they went on, and as soon as they reached\nthe water-edge recognised a large mob of blacks on the other side of the river.\nThe latter shouted out, \" Hullo ! you two-fellow ! what name ?\" (= what\ndo you want?), and got for answer, \" Me two-fellow look out pish (= fish, sect. 3).\nLeave him little-fellow place. Me two-fellow only got him small net.\" The\nnecessary permission having been granted, the two visitors went out into the middle\nof the water-hole and driving their hosts away, got all the fish for themselves and\nreturned to Booloo Booloo. When Mulkari asked them where they had got such\na fine haul, they told him a lie and said, \" Oh ! from little fellow water-hole, very\nmuddy,\" so that he should not guess the exact spot. Soon afterwards our two\nvisitors again went to Parapijori, and did exactly the same thing : they turned the\nwhole crowd of triendlies away, caught all the fish, and told a similar tale to\nMulkari on their return. They played this trick so often, that at last the Parapijori\nboys got into a temper and said, \" Me altogether-fellow kill him that two-fellow \" :\nthey therefore stuck some hook boomerangs (sect. 224) point upwards into the\nmud at the bottom of the water, and taking care to cast their nets earlier than\nusual, caught all the fish, and hid them behind some bushes. By-and-by, the two\nfishermen came up as usual, and noticing the tracks, exclaimed, \" Hullo ! you\nbeen catch him pish this morning,? \" in answer to which the crowd replied, \" No !\nme altogether-fellow no been catch him pish this morning. Big mob pelican and\nshag been playing about here and catch him all pish,\" and words to that effect. So\nthe pair went into the water, upon permit being granted, hunted the others away\nas before, but of course on this occasion caught no fish at all. At last when their\npatience was exhausted, the Pitta- Pitta said to the Yunda boy, \" You go dive\ndown,\" but the latter excused himself on account of his wearing a large head-net\n(sect. 168). After a bit of wrangling one of them eventually dived down, and as\nhe remained below the surface rather longer than customary, his mate, wondering\nwhat had happened, dived down too : directly both were out of sight, all the Parapijori\nmen jumped in, and having drowned them both, stuck them on to the hookboomerangs in the mud at the bottom.\n\n208. (h) The Porcupine and the Eagle-Hawk. — A porcupine and eagle-hawk\nwere fighting one day : the latter had a lot of spears which he stuck into the porcupine (the bristles), but by way of punishment he was made to eat raw meat.\n\n209. (j) The Black Crow and the Hawk. — A black crow and a hawk had a\nfight. The hawk succeeded in knocking his adversary over and rolling him in the\ncharcoal, whence his black plumage ; he himself got punished, however, by being\nmade to eat putrid meat.\n\n128 BECBEA.TION: COBBOBBOBEES, SFOBTS, JlSTD GAMES.\n\n210. (k) The Hawk and the Bower-bird. — There was a quarrel between a\nsmall hawk — the species with a \" dirty brisket \" — and* the bower-bird : the hawk\ngot the worst of it. So the hawk thought he would steal his opponent's young\nones and eggs, but going to the nest could only find grass and stones there\n(i.e., the play-ground) : he therefore left a snake in the enclosure which bit and\nkilled the bower-bird when he came home at night.\n\n211. (l) The Moon. — A long time ago, when the blackfellow was a turkey,\nhe damaged his foot and ankle very badly, and asked a gin, a cockatoo-parrot,\nwhere the nearest water-hole was. She said, \" No water here.\" He then asked\na green parrot if he knew where the water was, and as the foot was becoming\nmore swollen, requested him furthermore to cut it open, but the green-parrot\nsaid he couldn't do it. He thereupon successively appealed to a crow, a blackfellow doctor, an eagle-hawk, the moon, a white-fellow doctor, and even the\nevil-one himself, to render him the necessary assistance : but they one and all\nsaid they couldn't undertake the job. As a last chance he begged of the earthgrub to give him relief : the latter said he would, and thereupon bit into the\nswollen flesh, bored his way deep into the diseased part, sucked all the putrid matter\nout, and cured the patient. A large corrobboree was therefore held, and the galahs,\nstorm-birds, white and black cockatoos, butcher-birds, magpies, bower-birds, together\nwith the opossums, porcupines, bandicoots, &c, all took part in it. And while\nthe turkey and the earth-grub together with the clouds and skies shifted their\nposition (for the latter had until then always remained on the surface of the\nground) the whole party began singing \" there goes our brother up.\" And of\ncourse both animals stayed up there. But so that the people below should always\nremember what a good physician he had proved himself to be, the earth-grub\nsends a moon regularly every month to bear him in mind, for the moon is a\nbrother of his, and, like him, bores his way out of the ground, rises up again on\nhigh, sinks once more and dies. He has plenty of brothers, this worm, and so he\nsends a different one, a moon, every month. [N.B. — That it is a different moon\nevery month is a common belief among these aboriginals.]"

(m) The Galah-parrot and the Opossum. — A galah and an opossum,\neach having tomahawks, were fighting one day, with the result that they both\ngot very much damaged : the parrot got his neck and breast all cut open (red\nplumage), while the opossum received a black mark on his snout.\n\n213. Sometimes it is cut\ndown from one of the other kinds of boomerang that has been damaged or broken.\nIf coloured at all, it is smeared with charcoal : it may often be ornamented, but\nthere is no rule or uniformity in the gravings, of which some of the designs\nmay be very quaint (e.g., emus with net in Fig. 309, iguanas in Fig. 310). No\nfurther definitive description can be offered. The return boomerang is never used\nas a recognised article of exchange or barter : that is to say it does not travel,\nand is manufactured just as occasion requires. It is strictly a man's toy, and is\nused in different ways as follows : — In the Boulia District, five, six, or perhaps\nmore men will stand in Indian file, each individual with raised arms resting his\nhands on the shoulders of the one in front : another of the playmates, standing\nby himself at some distance ahead and facing the foremost of the file, throws the\nboomerang over their heads, and as it circles round they all follow it in its\ngyration, the game being for any of them to escape being hit, each taking it in\nturn to throw the missile (see bird's-eye view in Fig. 311). Among the Yaroinga\ntribe on the Upper Georgina, they often try and arrange to make up two sides,\nthe object being for a member of one team to hit an individual of the opposite\ngroup. In the Cloncurry District, the Mitakoodi fix a peg into the ground, and\nthe one who can strike or come nearest to it with the boomerang when it falls to\nthe ground is declared the best man."
}

The spin-ball is a round ball of about 1 to H inch diameter, made of lime,\nashes, sand, clay, and sometimes hair, rolled into shape either between the hands\nor the folds of a blanket, and subsequently baked, thus making it smooth and\nhard : it may subsequently be painted with red or yellow-ochre. It would appear to have been\nintroduced into these parts from the Lower Diamantina Biver, within but very\nrecent years, coming up the Georgina via Bedouri : it does not seem to have\nreached, or to be known, to the Mitakoodi as yet (1896). The Skipping-rope. — Among the Northern Mitakoodi and Grenada\nKalkadoon, a sort of skipping-rope, too-ri too-ri, is made from the long roots* of\ntho Bauhinia or of the big white-gum growing near the water's edge : the rope is\nheld by two play-mates, who swing it backwards and forwards — they do not\ncircle it.\n\n218. \"Hunt the Eye\" is played as follows: — On a small piece of level sandy\nground, a circular space of from 2 to 2\\ feet in diameter is roughly marked out,\nand carefully smoothed over with the hand. Hound this ring members of either\nsex and any age may be squatting, and all eyes being closed at a given signal, one\namongst the number will hide some small object beneath the sand which the others\nwill now set upon discovering. The object hidden is the lens of a rat's, opossum's,\nor small kangaroo's eye, removed after cooking ; indeed, the Kalkadoons speak of\nthis as the tnil-ti or \" eye \"-game, though, as a matter of fact, anything different\nfrom the constituents of the subjacent soil, e.g., seeds, &c, and of comparatively\nminute size, say, £ to i inch in diameter, may be used for the purpose. The players\nstart looking for the hidden object by picking up a pinch or two of sand at a\ntime, and letting it sift slowly through the fingers. Another way of playing\nthe game is for the original hider, while the others have their eyes open, to take\nlip handful after handful of sand and sprinkle it here and there rapidly over the\ncircular space : he watches his opportunity, and lets the object to be hidden fall\nwith the sand. \" Hunt the Eye \" is common throughout all the different\nethnographical districts.\n\n219. \" Hide and Seek \" is also a very commonly played game, even by adults.\nThere may be as many as three seekers in it, these covering their eyes with the\nhands, or putting their heads, with eyes shut, close to the ground while the others\nhide themselves. How a\nMessage-stick is put into Use.\n\n224. The \" Walk-about \" is perhaps, in its ultimate results, one of the most\nimportant institutions in vogue among the aboriginals, and yet one on account of\nwhich their white brethren will, as often as not, hold them up to ridicule and\ncontempt. To the settlers it is considered in the light of an excuse for a holiday\nor for shirking the work upon which the blacks would otherwise be employed :\npurmises that in pome cases may be perfectly correct. In the majority of instances,\nhowever, this walk-about is but part and parcel of the great trading or bartering\nsystem which is more or less continually going on throughout the various districts.\nCertain trade-routes laid down from time immemorial along their own or\nmessmates' country are followed by the members of a tribe or tribes, along which\neach knows that he is free to travel unmolested : these routes, of greater or less\nextent, are rigidly adhered to. The opening of the local market, so to speak,\nmay take place at the instance of one of the elders or \" bosses \" at one of the\nlarger camps, eg., Marion Downs, Port Constantino, (fcc, where instructions are\nissued as to when to leave, whom to go, what to take, and what to return with.\nIn smaller and less frequented encampments, e.g., Boulia, the peregrination may\ncommence when any fresh pituri is seen knocking about for sale, this being a\npretty certain indication that their neighbours elsewhere must all be on the walkabout themselves. It also often happens that an individual will start on the road\nfor business on his own, or friends' account, whenever the inclination suits.\n\nThe recognised routes invariably, and for reasons readily intelligible, run\nalong water-courses and water-holes ; taking all in all it may be stated that owing\nto the ordinarily scanty supplies of this commodity during the summer months, the 1\nwalk-about usually takes place sometime during the winter ones. The length of\ntime occupied on each journey varies with the distance of course, from a few\nweeks to several months, and cases are not unknown where the blacks will travel\nall one winter before reaching their destination, will spend the summer, the dry\nseason, there, and then return the following winter.\n\n225. Signs and Signals on the Road. — In connection with these peregrinations\ncertain methods are adopted for indicating the road or denoting the traveller's\npresence to friends and fellow-tribesmen in front or behind : such are the smoke -\nsignals, finger-posts, foot-prints, geopraphical names, terms for cardinal points,\n&c. Smoke-signals and signal-fires are known to have been recognised and\nanswered at distances upwards of ten miles apart. A variation is sometimes\nmade in \" breaking*' the smoke so as to make it rise in quickly succeeding\ncolumns : these smoke-breaks are made by lighting an ordinary fire in the open,\nbut alternately covering and removing with leafy boughs in rapid succession.\n\" Smoke-rings\" at Birdsville and the surrounding district are said to be produced\nby igniting some bushes placed inside a hollow log fixed up on end, on the top of\nof which a piece of bark is placed, this being quickly slipped off in the same\nhorizontal plane, and as speedily replaced when a \" ring\" is wanted : I have\nobserved nothing like this, however, around Boulia. In response to inquiry, it\nwould appear that no special information can be conveyed by these smoke-signals\nbeyond the actual presence there of the person or persons making them. Though\noutside human control, yet forming a very distinctive sign at long distance of the\npresence of a camping-ground, are the numerous small brown hawks which will\nfollow in the wake of the travellers for miles and miles : in the early days, these\nleathered scavengers have often proved the means of giving the aboriginals away\n\nfEATllL, TBADE, AITD BABTER. \" LETTER\" OB \" MESSAGE-STICK.\" 13S"

the actual footprints of the party preceding ; and in this connection it may be

  "passage_text": "228. Arrangements at the Camping-ground.— On the road a man will
travel by himself, unlike a woman, or in company. If women are present,
they bring up the rear with the children, well-stuffed dilly-bags ana other
possessions, the men at some distance ahead carrying their own' fighting
weapons. As the different parties reach their ultimate destination, -they take
up their quarters or build temporary huts around the visited, their hosts',
camp upon that side of it in the direction whence they came. Thus, in the
Pitta-Pitta camp at Boulia, if all arrangements were properly carried out,
the Miorli visitors from Springvale aud the Diamantina would settle down
on the eastern side of the Boulia-ites, the Yunda and Yellunga folk on the north,
the Marion Downs people on the south, &c. From the fact that a comparatively
large number of people of both sexes may be congregated at the various camps
and swapping-grounas, pleasure is often combined with business, new corrobborees
are performed and taught to others, or perhaps old ones exchanged, a general
holiday made of it, and the relaxation "thoroughly enjoyed. When acquaintances
meet, men and men, there may be a hand-shaking, but whether this is indigenous
or a habit derived from the whites I am unable to say. Instead of for sorrow,
tears may be made to flow, among the women-folk, for very gladness. Thus, a
not uncommon form of greeting, say, after some years' interval, between mother
and daughter, among the northern Kalkadoon of Quamby, &c., is for the elder
woman to take any heavy stick, a fighting-pole, and, digging into the top of her
head, rub it in there until the blood comes, crying and sobbing as much as she
can : the daughter from behind is all this time putting her arms round the old
woman's waist, and when she thinks that her mother has given way sufficiently to

. her feelings will forcibly take the stick away.

229. Trade Routes. — In the following notes relative to the trade-routes,
markets, &c, of some of the more important tribes of North- West-Central
Queensland, difficulty is here and there experienced in locating their chief home
or head -encampment owing to there being perhaps no station homestead marked
near enough on the maps to indicate accurately its geographical position : furthermore, the alienation from the aboriginals of their hunting-grounds, the hostility
of some of the station-managers, stockmen, &c., and other causes, have of late
years concurred, and still concur, in making appreciable changes in the lines of
travel. Information has been collected concerning the " markets" of the Boulia,
Upper Georgina, Leichhardt-Selwyn, and Cloncurry Districts, and in this order it
is proposed to deal with them.

230. (a) In the Boulia District, Pitta-Pitta blacks will travel vid Herbert
Downs to Glenormiston, and then either on to Carlo or to Roxburgh, returning the
same way to Boulia or Marion Downs. This is the route adopted when pituri is
required : the plant (sect. 147) grows in the neighbourhood of Carlo, whence
some of it is already taken over to Roxburgh vid the Toko Ranges. This same
tribe, the Pitta- Pitta, together with the Boinji and Yellunga, may also go along
the Burke and Wills Rivers to Buckingham Downs, Chatsworth, and Devoncourt
to return with spears and koolamons : others, in company or not with Kalkadoon
people, may continue their journey along the ranges to Rochdale and Carandotta,
returning home down the Georgina vid Herbert Downs and Parapijori, exchanging
Government blankets, pituri, human-hair belts, " bilbi"-tails, &c, for shields,

stone-knives, opossum twine, human-hair twine (sect. 162), and hand-spears. The
Yunda people will visit Boulia, Marion Downs, Cooraboolka, Springvale, Diamantina Gates, and following the river up to Kynuna and Dagworth, may sometimes
call in at McKinlay, and return home via Devoncourt and Chats worth : these take
or collect on the* road pituri, spears, opossum-twine, and boomerangs for the
Yellunga, Kalkadoon, and G-oa, obtaining in exchange stone-knives, spears, &c.
The Weelko, Kwokwa, and others, starting from Marion Downs, &c, travel up
the G-eorgina as far as Headingly, returning via Gordon's Creek, Walaya, Toko
water-hole, and Glenormiston : they barter all sorts of spears, ornate boomerangs
(sect. 241), Government blankets, &c, for lunga-lunga (sect. 212) and hookboomerangs (sect. 244), leaf -shaped wommeras (sect. 253), and long single-piece
spears, painted shields (sect; 254), pearl-shell, eagle-hawk feathers, grind-stones
(sect. 154), &c. The Miorli, from the neighbourhood of Springvale, may take a
Toad up the Diamantina as far as Cork, and, until a few years ago, or perhaps
still, cut across even to Acheron Creek, Tocal, and down the Thomson to Carella,
returning by the same route : they exchange lunga-lunga and hook-boomerangs,

(c) In the Leichhardt-Selwyn District, the Kalkadoon, said to be the most\nsavage of the aboriginals under consideration, travel southwards but verv short\ndistances outside their own immediate country.   "passage_text": "234. Transmission of Customs, Beliefs, and Language, &c. — This system of
inter-communication, necessitated by exchange and barter, is one to which far too
little importance appears to have been attached by European writers. In the
case, for instance, of implements, stress has hitherto been laid on the particular
locality whence they have been collected, rather than upon the particular tribe or
district which originally manufactured them. The presence in camp at Boulia of
opossum-hair and eagle-hawk feather ornaments (both- of which creatures are
almost extinct in the neighbourhood), mother-of-pearl and other marine shells, as
well as two curiously barbed spears (which I knew from previous evidence and
descriptions could only have come from one of the Northern Territory coast
tribes), led me on step by step to the inquiry as to how .these articles, as well as
others, reached their destination. The outcome of these investigations was that
the various recognised trade routes were gradually learnt, and the commodities
bartered at the different swapping-grounds enumerated. Mention has already been
made (sect. 228, &c.) how that comparatively large numbers of people of both sexes
may be congregated sometimes at these local markets. Thus it happens that
ideas are interchanged, superstitions and traditions handed from district to
district, and more or less modified and altered in transit, that new words and terms
are picked up, and that corrobborees are learnt and exchanged, just like any other
commodities. I have repeatedly obtained proofs of similar customs, beliefs,
corrobborees (sect. 191), &c, holding good among tribes separated by miles of
country which, except through the medium of others, had certainly not within the
white-man's memory ever been in communication. Thus, tribes occupying
territory at opposite extremes, and beyond them also, of a large district like
North-West-Central Queensland are brought into contact through the intermediation of others : indeed, so far as philology alone is concerned, it is matter for
wonder that there are comparatively so f evv, where we might have expected so many,
words with common-root stems among tribes undoubtedly speaking absolutely
different languages. Again, there is reason to believe that for future pioneers
and settlers into the far western, and what is still believed to be arid, country, a
knowledge of these aboriginal lines of travel or trade-routes* might prove of great
value, since only along them would there be a chance of finding water. Out
beyond the Toko Ranges, over large areas still awaiting exploration at the hands of
Europeans, the Undekerebina men, who were encamped at G-lenormiston during
my visit there, assured me of certain definite routes which they had themselves
followed— they knew all about the Central telegraph line in the sister colony,
which some of them had seen. Furthermore, it is quite within the realms of
probability that a careful study of the aboriginal trade-routes throughout the
various colonies (as in the analogous examples elsewhere of the migrations of
animals and birds) would throw no unimportant light upon that much- vexed
question as to the source of origin of the Australian aboriginal — whence he came
to be where he is now found.

^ 235. Letter or Message Sticks. — Circumstances often arise which may prevent
an individual setting out for the "swapping-ground" or local market, and in such
cases he may send a substitute or agent together with a so-called letter-stick to do
business for him. This letter or message stick is culled Jca-lor-i by the Pitta-Pitta
tribes, kool-bo by the Mitakoodi, and koong-ga by the Kalkadoon : in the lastmentioned language this word signifies a piece of wood of any description (e.g.,
sect. 161). The stick is usually a piece of wood, gidyea, ti-tree, or any other convenient, coloured perhaps black, red, or yellow, from two to four or more inches in

*h£ so-called "letteb" oe "message-stick." 137

length, cut to various shapes from flat to round, and incised with various marks or

patterns: occasionally, if the sender is in a hurry, or too lazy to manufacture one, it

may consist of some peculiarly-marked twig in the rough, a plain piece of wood

cut to shape, a small bundle of rags tied round and round with hair-string, twine,

or cotton, &c. It means nothing more than a sort of brand or mark belonging to

an individual whp, so long as he is able to recognise it again, or others for him,

can vary it at will in shape, size, or design : in other words, two which happen to

be totally unlike, may be accompaniments of the identical message. More than

anything else, the stick acts as a sort of guarantee of good faith, to show there is

"no gammon," and may at times act as a safeguard or passport over otherwise

hostile country : there is nothing on it in the form of a communication which can

actually be read, the substitute or messenger invariably carrying the message by

word of mouth. The messenger is in all cases an adult man, never a woman, and

a person, such as a brother, &c , whom it is known can be trusted. With regard

to the particular shapes and designs of these message-sticks, there are traces of

similarity even over large areas of country. In the Boulia District they are

flattened, generally thinner at the edges than elsewhere, rounded or more or less

pointed at the extremities, and incised only with straight lines. These straight

lines are cut either parallel with, at an angle, or across each other, and represent

q uite arbitrarily anything which the manufacturer chooses, from a mountain or a

river to a station homestead : sometimes, the comparatively large size of the head

station or chief encampment has been attempted in an extra number of lines or

cross lines. The back ot the message-stick bears the same or similar design as

"the front, or else is covered with " flash" marks, to make it look " pretty fellow" ;"
}

  "passage_text": "237. How a Message-stick is put into Use. — The message-stick may be put\ninto actual use as follows : — \" Charlie,\" residing at Boulia, we will say, wants\nsome pituri, but being employed at work from which he cannot be spared, or being\nsick, is prevented going for it himself: he therefore sends a brother of his,\n\" Peter,\" to the nearest market, which in this case would be Carlo, to get some for\nhim. Peter takes the stick which Charlie has just made, and journeying trid\nHerbert Downs and Glenormiston arrives at his destination on the Mulligan River\nwhere, being asked his business, he says that he has come for pituri, and hands in\nthe message- stick. In reply to questions he will mention who it is that has sent\nhim — namely, Charlie of Boulia — and may be then informed by his inquisitor, \" No,\nI can't let you have any. I have two or three letter-sticks here already, waiting\nfor pituri, and I must serve them first. Go and ask that fellow over there.\"\nApproaching the person indicated, he is asked as before, what he wants and whom\nhe comes from : having satisfied the vendor as to his bona Jides, the latter takes\ncharge of the stick and tells him he can supply him in a few days' time, Peter in\nthe meantime making friends with some \" brother\" or \" sister\" in the local camp.\nA dilly-bag- full of pituri being at last forthcoming, it is handed over with the\nletter- 8 tick (which the vendor has been taking careful mental note of, so as to\nrecognise again), and Peter takes his departure back to Charlie at Boulia. Charlie,\non receipt of the parcel, will now forward some boomerangs, spears, a Government\nblanket, &c, in payment : if he can get Peter to take a second trip all well and\ngood, but if not, as is generally the case for such a journey, he gets another\nmessenger with the goods and the identical message- stick as before. ' This second\nmessenger arriving at - Carlo, finds the vendor, and hands him over the goods\ntogether with the stick : recognising the latter the seller accepts the various\narticles in payment for the particular bag-full of pituri which he had parted with\nsome few weeks previously, knowing now that he has been paid by the right party\n(probably personally unknown to him) — i.e., the sender of the original stick. But\nsupposing he never gets paid, or does not receive what he considers to be sufficient,\nhe will bear the fact well in mind that Charlie of Boulia is a bad character not to\nbe depended on, and take good care that neither he nor his friends have any\ndealings with him in the future. The seller, under circumstances such as have\nbeen just narrated, does not, as a rule, ask for the particular commodities he\nexpects to exchange, each head-encampment having its own special and well-known\nline of goods. Instead of trade or barter, the letter-stick may be sent round with\nany ordinary message or private communication, as already mentioned in the notes\nto illustrations (sect. 236)."

Nulla-Nullas. 257. Stone-Knives. 258.\nStone-Tomahawks.\n\n238. The Maintenance of Law and Order: Methods of Fighting. — Among the\nPitta- Pitta and other tribes of the.Boulia District, the paucity of old men whose\nopinions and wishes would otherwise be respected and enforced, is very marked.\nEach individual, within certain limits, can do what he pleases. On the other hand,\nhe has to reckon not only with the particular person injured, or his relatives, but\nalso, in some cases, with the whole camp collectively. Thus the camp as a body,\nas a camp council, will take upon itself to mete out punishment in crimes of\nmurder, incest, or the promiscuous use of fighting-implements within the precincts\nof the camping-ground : death, and probably the digging of his own grave, awaits\nthe delinquent in the former case, while \" crippling,\" generally with knives, constitutes the penalty for a violation of the latter. Private quarrels are arranged\nand settled somewhat on the following lines : — Supposing an individual considers\nhiuiself aggrieved, an animated conversation ensues between the parties concerned,\nobscene language is freely used (sect. 333), the hand goes up to the mouth in the\ncustomary manner (sects. 103, 104), and all of a sudden, probably a boomerang\nis let fly, to be followed or replied by another or similar implement. Mutual\nfriends, or their gins, will, in nine case out of ten, next intervene, and make an\nattempt at separating the pair: otherwise, they will each run for the nearest spear\nor anything handy, and throw it. Success may or may not attend the efforts of\n\"the peace- makers, but the truce, if one exists, is usually only temporary, for each\ncombatant may have concealed in his waist -belt a stone-knife, which in clos^\nquarters can play terrible mischief. If the feud is going to develop into anything j\nserious, both parties will probably betake themselves to a distance from camp. In'\nfighting thus as the outcome of a private quarrel, there is actually, as a rule, no j\nintention of killing, the risk, as will be shown further on, being too greatj.h\n\"With two-handed swords, they would only aim at striking each other oAfi\n\"the head : with spears, they* would only make for the fleshy parts off\n\"the thighs: with stone-knives, they would only cut into the snouldersj\nflanks, and buttocks, producing gashes an inch or more deep, and up to\nseven or even eight inches long. In using the last-named implement, the\none individual may grapple the other, standing or sitting, very much after the\nmanner of a person wrestling (Fig. 339). Clasping his opponent with the one\nhand, he holds the knife in the other, and sticks it into one of the localities\npermitted ; with a turn of the wrist he gives jag for jag, as a rule, he t removing\nthe blade from the wound. Accidents sometimes occur, and an incision is made\nunfairly — that is, outside one of the recognised spots : thus, during a fight with\nstone-knives at Glenormiston in 1894, \" Toko Tommy,\" a visitor from the\nTJndekerebina tribe, when remonstrated with for inflicting a very ugly cut into the\nback of his adversary's knee, excused himself by maintaining \"Charlie, silly\n\nb : he move him leg,\" insinuating by this. remark that it was the fault of his\n\nopponent in shifting his position. The lying upon the back on the ground, a\n\nSosture in which no lawful incisions with a stone-knife can be made, is the sign of\nefeat — that the combatant has had enough, and gives in. Even while a fight is\ngoing on, the gins belonging to the two individuals in combat, as well as others,\nmay nave a set-to among themselves not only with their tongues but with fighting-\n\n140 THE MAINTENANCE OF LAW AND OEDEB :\n\npoles, (fcc, and what with the shouting and screaming of the women, the crying of\nthe children, coupled with the cheering and yelling of the other spectators, make\nyeritably a temporary pandemonium of the scene. At Glenormiston, the women\ncoming up to join a fray give a sort of war-whoop : they will jump up in the air,\nand as their feet, a little apart, touch the ground, they knock up the dust and\nsand with the fighting-pole, &c, held between their legs, very like one's early\nreminiscences in the picture-books of a witch riding a broom-stick. Before\nfighting commences, the combatants usually strip off even that little which they\nordinarily wear. As a rule they are very proud of these wounds received in fight,\nbut they apparently only very rarely take steps to elevate them above the level of\nthe surrounding surface, as in the case of the \" flash\" scars on the chest, &c.\n(sect. 186)."

If the victor turns out to be the aggrieved party he\nhas to show good cause, as for instance that the mau whom he has just taken\nupon himself to punish, had raped his gin, gave him the munguni (sect. 259, (fcc.),\nor wrought him some similarly flagrant wrong : under such circumstances, no\nfurther action is taken by anyone. If, on the other hand, the victor happens to\nbe the aggrieved party only in his own opinion, and not in that of those to whom\nhe is answerable, and who do not believe the grounds on which ho commenced the\nfight to be sufficient, he has to undergo exactly the same mutilations subsequently\nat the hands of the vanquished as he himself had inflicted: it devolves upon his\n\"brother\" to bring him back to undergo the punishment, though if a coward he may\nrun away from camp, but he dare then never return. Thus, in all these individual\nquarrels or fights, whatever injury may be perpetrated upon the vanquished, the\nlatter, supposing he has justice on his side — and this is regulated by the general\nopinion or the elders in camp — has the opportunity always afforded him of\nretaliating by similar injury with similar weapon — \" an eye for an eye, a tooth for\na tooth.\"\n\nIt occasionally happens that party feeling runs very high, and perhaps the\n\"brothers\" — and there may be dozens of these (sect. 59) on either side— take up the\nquarrel, which may hence lead to the whole camp, men as well as women, joining\nindiscriminately in the general melee. To prevent such occurrences, determined\nefforts are always made to nip a quarrel in the bud.\n\nSometimes, in the original duel, one of the combatants may be killed, and\nunless the survivor can show that he had sufficient provocation or cause, he will\nbe put to death in similar manner, at the instance of the camp-council, and usually\nundergo the extra degradation of digging his own as well as his victim's grave.\nIt may happen, however, that the person slain belongs to some neighbouring tribe,\nand consequently some time will elapse before the retribution falls, deservedly or\notherwise, upon the slayer. The deceased's friends, brothers, &c, when the news\nreaches them, will come up and demand the culprit, delivery of whom is usually\ngiven, considering that the request is generally backed by a formidable array of\nwarriors. The individual in question has now to stand single-handed the onslaught\nof his late victim's partisans — a sort of \" running the gauntlet.\" If spears are\nthrown he is allowed a shield wherewith to defend himself ; if fighting-sticks are\nemployed he is given the use of one : sometimes by accident or design — i.e., the\njudicious gift of various presents to the ringleaders in the latter case — he may\nstand the test successfully and escape with his life. But the occasion now and\nagain arises where not even with the actual death of the destroyer are the friends\nof the deceased individual satisfied : they may require delivery of another man to\nmake up for their loss, as it were, and if refused will fight collectively, with the\nresult that not unfrequently more or less are slain. There are times when the\nhomicide may get information privately concerning some expedition being on the\nroad after him, but to his credit, be it said, he will very rarely try to escape : if\ncourage should fail him, and he makes a bolt of it, he does so with the full\nknowledge of being ostracised for ever. If they have\nboth been made by the same person they are very probably similarly marked : if\nhe barters them, he will generally \" swap\" them only as a pair, though beyond\nthe fact of two being required as an accompaniment for beating time at the singsongs and the corrobborees, it is difficult to understand why this should so often be\nthe case.   "passage_text": "The longitudinal figures, invariably present, and reaching from tip to tip,\nconsist of straight lines, single or composite (Figs. 343, 344,a), and elongate ovals\nstrung end on end : the former would appear to be absent in weapons manufactured in or to the north of the Leichardt-Selwyn Ranges, by the Kalkadoon\nand Mitakoodi, for instance. The ovals, from their resemblance to things which\nthey most nearly approach, may be spoken of as shuttles and festoons. The\nfestoons, only found on implements made in and to the south of the Boulia\nDistrict, are limited to the extreme edges of the weapon (Figs. 344, 345, b) : their\ninterstices are filled up with parallel concentric lines, concavity outwards, so as to\nrepresent ripples on the water's edge, and hence in the Pitta-Pitta language are\nspoken of as the nar-pi ming-ka-ra, or river-bank marks. The shuttles (Pigs.\n314, 345, 346, c) are similarly filled in with more or less longitudinal lines, and are\nnamed as follows: — In the Boulia District, according to some native authorities,\nthey are called mol-lo-ro or mountain-tops, but the general consensus of opinion\nis that they represent the large fishing nets folded up for purposes of transit,\nand hence are described as ma-li ming-ka-ra or fishing-net marks. In the\nCloncurry District the shuttles, when their enclosed lines are strictly longitudinal\nas just described, are known as gin-ja-la or leaves ; when inclined to a distinct\nslant (Fig. 347d) they are called che-ka-ra or white-shell (sect. 182) marks. In\nthe Leichhardt-Selwyn District, I could obtain no local terms for them. As in\nthe case with the longitudinal lines, there may be one, two, or even three strings\nof these shuttles running the length ef the weapon.\n\nThe transverse figures (those stretching across the breadth of the boomerang)\nnot met with outside the Boulia District, are limited to the markings at the\nextremities, and at the centre, though in either case they are not invariably present.\nThe former, which are far more common, are constituted of from one to three or\nfour more or less parallel lines (Pigs. 343, 344, e), and known in {he Boulia\nDistrict as tin-ja (sect. 131) ming-ka-ra or handle-marks : they are met with again\non the nulla-nullas (sect. 256) and fighting-poles (sect. 255), and are primarily\nintended to act as a support to prevent the hand from slipping. The central\ngravings which, commencing somewhat south of Boulia, at »Springvale, &c, are\nmost usually found on the Diamantina weapons, consist either of two lines placed\nparallel or crosswise : in the latter case (Fig. 349a-b) forming two triangles with\napices in contact, the two areas enclosed being often subdivided into secondary\nspaces, each of which, independently of its neighbour, is filled with closely\nparallel lines. There is a similar subdivision into secondary spaces, &c, of the\narea enclosed by the two parallel lines (Pig. 348). It should be borne in mind\nthat these central transverse gravings do not by any means entail bilateral symmetry\non the complete design.\n\nIn the Boulia District, among the simpler interstitial figures — i.e., those\noccupying the intervening gaps left by the preceding longitudinal and transverse\nones — may be described the kangaroo (Figs. 343, 346, 347, f) and emu (Pig. 350o)\ntoe-tracks, with their two and three digits respectively, called in consequence the\nma-choom-ba and kool-pa-ri marks in the Pitta-Pitta language. Other marks are the\nfollowing : — The koodija-koodija represents the female flash-mark of red or yellow\nochre (sects. 185, 193) smeared over the thighs, legs, trunk, and arms, by means of\nthe three middle fingers dipped into the paint: this \"brand\" which, by-the-by, is\nnever spoken of as a snake, as might have been expected, is in exceptional cases\ncut across the entire width of the blade (Pig. 845n). The koo-ding-be-ri or single\nzigzag line is formed of circumflex accents, each made with two separate cuts,"

the style of the teeth in a saw : its native name would appear to have no other
interpretation attached to it. The ka-ta-pa ka-ta-pa (Fig. 350l) and me (Fig.
placed end on end with more or less regular precision (Fig. 350k), somewhat after
350m) marks are made with six and four separate incisions respectively; the
former signifies a hornet or bee, the latter an eye. The wer-Jcoo. or cross-cut
(Fig. 346ir) is identical with that made on the thighs of near male-relatives in
times of mourning (sect. 289) : the same mark is also locally described sometimes
as indicative of Marion Downs, situated, as it is, at the "crossing" of the two rivers,
the Hamilton and the Georgina. It must not be forgotten that of all the
preceding types of interstitial incisions it is exceptional to find more than two or
three varieties upon a boomerang at one and the same time. In the Leichhardt-
Selwyn and Cloncurry Districts the interstitial marks are limited to the kangarootoe type and the feather-pattern line. The former, up here, appears to have no
further meaning than- "two-fellow anything" : the latter is composed of
circumflex accents placed vertically . and parallel (Fig. 350o), and is known as
the Icoon-ya lcoon-ya (sect. 153), a grass- woven dilly-bag.

242. The Fluted Boomerang (Fig. 352) is not made at Boulia. Its home is

"beyond Noranside, at Buckingham Downs, Mount Merlin, Chatsworth, &c, and

along the Upper Georgina, certainly as far as Lake Nash, and out westwards from

"this river along the Toko Banges, and so into Central Australia: indeed this

^particular weapon may be said to be peculiar to the Leichhardt-Selwyn and Upper

Oeorgina Districts, For purposes of exchange and barter, it travels both up and

clown the Oeorgina : in the former case branching on the way eastwards across to

"the Mitakoodi of the Cloncurry District, in the latter making its way to the

^Mulligan and the Burke, whence vid Springvale it may journey both up and down

"the Diamantina. This weapon is invariably coloured red with ochre grease, and

made either of gidyea or " white-wood." As a rule it is shorter by 2 or 3 inches

than the ornate variety of the Boulia District, and, unlike it, the bend or knee, its

^widest part, is never exactly at the centre, while the extremities, or fips, without

exception, are always rounded. The upper convex side invariably, and the lower

flattened one very often, is completely covered with a distinct longitudinal fluting,

each flute being about an eighth of an inch wide, though the width would seem to

increase proportionately with the further north the locality of manufacture: in all

(*ases, the fluting is always wider and coarser on the under than on the upper

surface. At Bedouri, Birdsville, and on the Lower Georgina is manufactured a

fluted and red-coloured boomerang which is long, thin, inclined to be pointed at

the extremities, and is more or less rounded in section, though the tendency to

flattening on the under surface is fairly marked : this weapon, the pa-run-da, is

very rarely, and then only accidentaly, met with at Boulia, its route being in an

opposite direction, southwards down the Diamantina.

243. The Plain Boomerang, with its surfaces perfectly smoothed, and coloured
black with charcoal, comes from the Cloncurry District, where it is named after
the gidyea wood of which it is made, the pa-je-ra (sect. 239.) Whether the
Kalkadoon obtain this implement in barter from their Mitakoodi neighbours, or
make it themselves, is doubtful, though the fact of their having a name of their
own for it, the ma-ra-bil-la (sect. 239), renders the latter supposition a little likely.
In reply to inquiry in the Boulia District, a "plain " boomerang is always looked
upon in the light of one incompleted. The Cloncurry District plain boomerang
averages between 29 and 30 inches from tip to tip, with the proximal end markedly
narrower than the distal : it has no signs of a fluting, but in most cases' the
extremities are " angled" off for flash purposes.

244. The Hook Boomerang (Fig. 353) has the same destination as the fluted
variety, which it resembles both in fluting and in colour : it is made chiefly in the
Upper Georgina Districts by the Workia and Yaroinga especially. It differs from
the, fluted boomerang in the possession of a hook, the "ear" of the Boulia and
Toko Ranges, tribes, from 4 to 5 inches long projecting backwards, in the same
plane, from the extremity of the shaft on the convex edge : this hook, about an
inch or more wide at its base, tapers gradually to a blunt point, and bears a longitudinal fluting continuous with that on the main shaft. Furthermore, the shape

of the shaft contrasts markedly with that of all other boomerangs in its width,
independently of the bend or knee (wotf.its widest part), increasing progressively
from the proximal to the hooked extremity. Its use has already been drawn
attention to in sect. 240, while the various names applied to it are given in sect.
239. Besides being used as a fighting weapon, the Workia employ the hookboomerang for throwing into flying mobs of flock-pigeons (sect. 13v)."

The Two-handed Sword is manufactured at Boulia, Warenda, Herbert\nDowns, Marion Downs, and south of this on portions of the Diamantina — i.e., in\nthe Boulia District only, so far as North -West-Central Queensland is concerned.\nIt travels northwards, up the Georgina, where it is bartered for fluted and hook\nboomerangs, peg-tipped spears, and other things. Made from gidyea, and\nsubsequently blacked with charcoal, it varies from 3 J to over 4 feet in length.\nIt is curved, though not so markedly, after the manner of a boomerang, which it\nfurther resembles in being wider at the middle than at the extremities ; both\nsurfaces are convex, one being very much more so than the other, and its tips are\nalways evenly rounded. Only one side, the more convex, is ornamented with\ngravings which, according to the orthodox fashion, are of the following pattern : —\nThis, in the main, consists of groups of parallel bars running lengthways with the\nimplement, the number of separate groups varying from five or six to as many as\na dozen (Figs. 354, 355, 356, 357, 358, a), and the number of contained bars from\nthree to five or six : furthermore, each bar is itself composed of from three to\nsometimes half-a-dozen closely applied parallel longitudinal lines. Transversely\ncut gravings may sometimes be seen either at the centre of the weapon (Figs. 356,\n357, 358, b) or else dividing off the separate groups of bars into compartments\n(Fig. 355c) : generally speaking, these are either of an angular or curved type.\nAt one or both extremities, handle-marks may be met with in the form of cross-cuts\n(Fig. 354d), dashes (Fig. 355e), or transverse lines (Fig. 356r). Any really\ncurvilinear longitudinal incisions are extremely rare, if they ever occur : only on\none occasion, at Roxburgh, on a disused and broken implement, did I see any\ntraces of the festoons, shuttles, &c, met with on the Boulia District ornate\nboomerangs. Otherwise, than for these gravings, the two-handed sword or\nun-ti-ti-ri has a smooth surface throughout, unless we except the purposely or\naccidentally left slight longitudinal fluting on the less convex surface. From\" the\nfact that this weapon when in use is held at either extremity with both hands,\nthe concave edge being the cutting one, the two surfaces cannot be spoken of as\nupper or under.\n\n246. Spears. — In the Boulia District, when any extra good spear is made, or\nwhen one has been proved to aim true, &c, it is often ornamented more or\nless in its whole length with a very fine longitudinal fluting : such an one is not\neasy for white strangers to get hold of. Both here and elsewhere — e.g., north of\nthe Selwyn Ranges — spears may be painted with alternate red and white bars for\nflash purposes. No spears whatever are manufactured round Bedouri and down\ntowards Birdsville : whatever are found there are brought in exchange and barter.\nThe names for spears of any kind in general, throughout the different\nethnographical districts, are given in the table in sect. 55. The different varieties\nof spears in particular (with their local terms) met with throughout North-\nWest-Centrai Queensland will now be detailed.\n\n247. The Acicular-tip Hand-spear.— The ma-ri-rno of the Boulia District\n(Fig. 359) is a hand-spear from 8 to 10 feet long, made in one piece, circular in\nsection from butt to tip, which is tapering and sharply pointed : the butt also\ngradually tapers off. The material from which this spear is cut is either gidyea,\n\" dead-finish\" scrub (Acacia farnesiana, Willd., Albizzia basaltica, Benth.), a\nspecies of rosewood, &c. It is manufactured in the Boulia, Leichhardt-Selwyn,\nCloncurry, and Flinders Districts, including the country around the Upper\nDiamantina from its very source. Occasionally, previous to fighting, some\ncementing substance, spinifex- or beefwood-gum, is stuck on in the form of a\nring about £ inch thick at a distance of, perhaps, a couple of feet from the tip :\ninto this band some iron nails, pieces of flint or glass, &c, may be found stuck\nThis spear is bartered on the one hand northwards along the Upper Georgina,"
}

  "passage_text": "FIGHTING. FIGHTING- WEAPONS. 147\n\nand on the other southwards along the Lower Diamantina. The Mitakoodi call\nit me-ri-mo or ne-ri-mo, the Goa tun-doo-roo-la. The position of the hand when\nin the act of throwing this and similar hand-spears is shown in Fig. 144, the\nweapon being balanced on the palm and along the length of thumb.\n\n248. The Spatnlate-tip Hand-spear. — The tum-ba-ra spear (Fig. 360) of the\nBoulia District, which, like the preceding, is a hand one, differs from it in having\na spatula te, instead of a gradually tapering, tip : this blade, which locally undergoes\nmodification both in shape and size, so far as comparative width (up to 2 inches)\nto length (up to 30 inches) is concerned, may sometimes be seen decorated with\na bilinearly parallel and sinuous red pattern on a white background (Fig. 361a.).\nThe butt also tapers off somewhat. The weapon reaches to a length of about a\nfoot shorter than the marimo, is similarly made in one piece of the same materials,\nand goes on transit along identical tracts of country. Among the Mitakoodi this\nspear is called e-ra-ka-la . ov ji-ni-bur-i : a curious fact in connection with the\nformer name is that the same word in the Pitta- Pitta language signifies ■\" flat,\"\nand in all probability refers to its spatulate tip. In this same tribe, the base of\nthe blade may have a mitre-form pattern graved upon it (Fig. 361b). Here and\nthere I have come across extra long examples of this spear, especially designed for\nkilling cattle.\n\n249. The Spatnlate-tip Wommera Spear. — The per-cha ma-ro, literally signifying \" peg-possessor \" in the Pitta-Pitta language, is among the heaviest of the\nwommera-thrown spears. It is well over 3 feet long, and made of three pieces,\nwhich may be spoken of respectively as the butt, the shaft, and the tip. The\nshaft is the only portion of the weapon which is ever ornamented, if at all, with a\nlongitudinal fluting, and is made of some particular wood, e.g., inulga, which will\ngive strength, weight, and stability : it is very firmly attached by splicing and the\nordinary spinifex cementing substance, &c, with the butt, and only very loosely\nwith the tip. The butt is made of any light kind of timber, e.g., \" cork\" wood\n{Erythrina, Linn.), or a piece of pine when obtainable, and is iu tended to impart\nthe proper direction required when throwing : at its free extremity is the small\nconcavity for the wommera to fit into. The spatulate tip, between 16 and 17\ninches long (Figs. 362, 363), on to one surface of which the rounded, almost halfmoon-shaped wooden hook is firmly bound, is fixed loosely into the shaft for a\ntwofold reason : to increase the difficulties of extraction when once the leverage\nis removed, and to prevent the butt or shaft being broken in view of its being\nrequired on a future occasion. The above explanations of the mechanism were\ngiven me by some Pitta-Pitta blacks. These spears are made in the Upper\nQ-eorgina district from Glenormiston onwards ; westwards, the Undekerebina use\nthem ; and eastwards, they may sometimes be met with among the Kalkadoon, who\nprobably also make them.\n\n250. Wommera Reed-spears. — The li-bi-ja-ra of the Cloncurry District is a\nreed-spear, very heavy and long, sometimes over 12 feet, and thrown with a\nwommera. It is composed of a butt and shaft. The butt, made of reed, takes up\nabout half or slightly less than the length of the entire weapon : into ita hollow\n(Fig. 364a) is fixed the thin gidyea shaft, the union of the two being strengthened\nwith beef -wood gum and a few turns of tendon. The tip ends in a gradually tapering point, like the marvmo. When in the act of being thrown with the wommera\nin one hand, the spear itself is supported on the other, which is extended forward.\n\nThe ma-ba-na is even thicker, longer, and heavier than the preceding, but\notherwise of similar construction, and wommera-thrown. It used to be manufactured out Mullangera way, but is very rarely to be met with now anywhere ; it was\noriginally designed for the spearing of cattle.\n\nThe ki-tu-ma and ja-loon, also of the Cloncurry District, are both of them\nsmaller, and comparatively lighter, varieties of the libijara ; on an average they\nare about 7£ feet long, and thrown with wommeras. In the ja-loon, the reed -butt\nis almost twice as long as the gidyea, \"dead-finish\" scrub, or \" needle- bush\"\nshaft; with the kituma, the reverse is the case, the shaft being always very much\nlonger than the butt.\n\n148 THE MAINTENANCE OP LAW AND OBDEH :\n\nThe particular water-reed (kin-di in the Mitakoodi language) out of which\nthe butts of these particular Cloncurry District spears are manufactured is not\ntoo commonly to be found ; but as a rule is brought over from Woolgar and\nsurrounding neighbourhood, where it is bartered for. A similar reed grows,\nperhaps, along the upper reaches of the Burke and Wills ; at all events, the small\nkun-dor-a (so-called by the Pitta- Pitta aboriginals) reed-spear, which comes dpwn\nfrom these rivers to Boulia occasionally (but which, unfortunately, I have not\npersonally handled) appears to be identical with the Jtituma or jaloon of the\nCloncurry tribes. Again, one or two hooks may be attached to any or all of\nthese and the preceding reed-spears. This hook (pril-ja in the Mitakoodi\nlanguage, of. per-cha in the Pitta- Pitta) is cut out from \" wild currant \" bush, &c,\nabout 4 inches long, in the shape of a slightly curved sort of thin pencil gradually\ntapering to a point at each extremity ; it is fixed on to the very tip of the spear\n(Fig. 364b) with beef-wood gum bound round with tendon obtained xrom\nkangaroo-tail, emu-leg, or snake-neck. The second hook, when present, is fixed\nsimilarly a few inches below the first."

  "passage_text": "251. The Quartz-tip Wommera Reed-spear.— -The yun-ba-ra wommera-spear is\nmet with among the Northern Mitakoodi, whence it may be bartered to the\nKalkadoon around Grenada and surrounding country ; though it is sometimes\nmade by the former, it is most commonly manufactured by the blacks around\nSevan n ah. It reminds one very much of the libijara, being 11 feet long and\nupwards, with the reed-butt and gidyea shaft of about equal lengths, but differs\nin the get-up of the gradually tapering tip (Fig. 365), upon which are fixed with\nbeef-wood gum some ten or twelve small chips of white quartz placed oppositely\nto another set, very much after the style of the teeth in a lady's small hair-comb.\nThe Mitakoodi call this white quartz-stone yung-un-da-ra, whence another name\nfor this spear is sometimes derived.\n\n252. Non-indigenous -Spears. — In addition to all the spears just described as\nbeing indigenous to North- Western-Central Queensland, there are others occasionally met with, especially on its northern and north-western confines, which come\nin through exchange and barter. Thus at Coolullah, on the Upper Leichhardt River\n(sect. 127), I met with certain hand-spears for catching fish, &c, bearing at their\nextremities barbed prongs of sharpened wood or filed iron-wire (Fig. 366) : these\nbelonged to some Karunti boys who had come down* from the other side of\nNormanton. So again at Camooweal are found various form* of stone and\nbarb-tipped spears of foreign origin which have reached their destination from\nmore northerly and more westerly districts.\n\n253. Wommeras. — The various names applied to the wommera^in the different\nethnographical districts are tabulated in sect. 55.\n\nThe wommera manufactured in the Boulia, Leichhardt-Selwyn, and Cloncurry Districts ia of the nature of a thin, straight lath of gidyea, about\n2i feet long, f-inch thick, and 1£ inches wide, the width (in the Boulia District)\nbeing pretty constant in its entire length. So far as the width of the shaft is\nconcerned, it should be noted that as one travels northwards from Boulia into\nKalkadoon and Mitakoodi country, this becomes markedly increased, up to\n2 inches and more, at the centre as compared with the extremities (Pigs. 367, 368).\nThe thinner the lath, the better is the weapon considered. The surfaces are\nslightly and equally convex, but no graving or fluting has been noticed ; sometimes\na kind of decoration is produced by tying a string spirally round and colouring\nthe parts, left exposed, over a fire. The free extremity is rounded off,\nwhile the opposite one is cut off at more or less of a right angle, and in\nthe Boulia District two holes .pierced or burnt in it (Pig. 369) : when pierced,\nthese holes are drilled with a sharpened emu or kangaroo borie, and by\nthis means, and with tendon, &c, the peg tied on, its fixture being rendered\nstill more complete by a subsequent covering of the usual cementing substance\nof spinifex or beef-wood gum. Outside the Boulia District, the peg is fixed\non without any holes whatsoever, some tendon or twine with cement being used\ninstead. It is this peg or hook (the per-cha again of the Pitta Pitta) which\nfits into the concavity at the butt-end of the spear. It may be noted that this\n\nLIGHTING. FIGfiTING-WEAPONS. 149\n\nwommera, the whirler (sect. 2L5), and the chekara-shell chest-ornament (sect.\n182) are the only examples of aboriginal workmanship in these parts of the\ncountry, in which \" drilling\" is employed. The weapon is handled by fixing it\nbetween the fore-finger and middle digit, clasping its free end on to the palm with\nthe middle, ring, and little fingers, and at the same time guiding, or rather\nsteadying, the spear between the fore-finger aud thumb (Fig. 370).\n\nAmong the Northern Mitakoodi of Clonagh, &c, and Northern Kalkadoon\nof Grenada, (fcc, the following variety of wommera made of gidyea, iron- wood\n(Acacia excelsa, Benth.), &c. is very commonly met with, though not actually\nmanufactured by them. It differs from the preceding pattern in having a sort of\nhaft to prevent the hand slipping off (Fig. 371) : this haft, projecting at an\nangle from the same edge as the peg, is composed of a flattened ovate piece of\nbeef- wood gum, about 3 inches or more in its greater diameter ; a white piece of\nshell, the che-ka-ra (sect. 182) of the Mitakoodi language, with convex side outwards, is fixed on to both sides of it. Occasionally, a smaller chip of similar shell\nis fixed into the cement at the peg-end of the weapon. The width of the shaft is\ngreater at the centre than at the extremities. This form of wommera reaches its\ndestination here through the Nouun tribe at Mullangera, who obtain the shell\nfrom the Karunti, &c, people at Normanton. The ta-poon is the name (given me\nat Clonagh) of the spear belonging originally to this particular form of wommera,\nand which is bartered with it at the same time."

  "passage_text": "In the Upper Qeorgina District, certainly on the Upper Mulligan and\nUpper Georgina Rivers, and along the Toko Ranges, another kind of wommera\n(Big. 372) is manufactured, totally different to the preceding lath- types : its\nparticular name at Roxburgh among the Walookera tribe is yum-ma-ra (sect.\n55). The whole implement is very much shorter, just a little over 2 feet being\na very fair average. The shaft is flattened out in the shape of a leaf, slightly\nconcave, both lengthways and crossways like a spoon, about 6 inches at its\ngreatest width, and about ^-inch in thickness : its concavity may be used as a\n\" pituri-plate \" — i.e., to mix the pituri on — and traces of the greenish-yellow\nstains from this plant are very generally perceptible. The shaft may be\ndecorated further with a charcoal pattern of two parallel and sinuous lines, or\nwith gravings in the shape of concentric circles ; often a few transverse incisions\nare seen on the handle-end. The handle is covered with the usual cementing\nsubstance, into the extremity of which (Fig. 372a) is stuck a little piece of flint,\nwhich constitutes a \"sharpener\" when the spear-tip becomes blunted. At the\nopposite end of the weapon is a small half -moon- shaped peg (Fig. 372b), fixed on\nwith tendon, &c, and cementing substance. When in use for spear-throwing, it\nis clutched between the fore and middle fingers, &c, as in the manner already\ndescribed, but the plane of the shaft is held vertically, so as to afford least\nresistance to the air in the movement forwards. Sometimes, in close quarters, this\nwommera may be held by the handle and employed like a short single-handed\nsword : the nearest district where I have come across a true single-handed short\nsword is in the neighbourhood of Normanton, where the Wollangama call it\nroong-ha-ren. There are thus four different uses to which this \" leaf\" variety of\nimplement can be applied : a wommera, pituri-plate, sharpener, and sword. The\nBoulia District aboriginals cannot use this form of weapon fur throwing spears.\n\n254. Shields (for their various names, see sect. 55) are manufactured at\nRoxburgh and along the Upper G-eorgina, and in the Leichhardt-Selwyn and Cloncurry Districts : Noranside, in the Boulia District, is said to be the only locality\ntherein where they can be made — i.e., where suitable timber is met with. For\npurposes of trade and barter, those from the Upper Georgina come down the\nriver direct for the Lower Diamantina, a few branching off on the way from\nRoxburgh, &c, across country to the Toko Ranges, &c, or indirectly for the\nMiddle Diamantina, vid Boulia, Springvale, and Diamantina Gates. Shields\nmade in the Leichhardt-Selwyn and Cloncurry Districts may travel to the Upper\nDiamantina.\n\n\" The timber employed in the manufacture of a shield is the \"coral\" or \"cork--\ntree {Erythrina, Linn.), or other soft and light wood, the name of the particular\nmaterial sometimes being identical with that of the weapon, e.g., Pitta-Pitta koonpa-ra = cork-tree, shield, koolamon.\n\n150 THE MAINTENANCE OP LAW AND ORDER :\n\nIf the tree be a small one the required length of trunk may be cut off,\nand one shield made : if larger, it may be split longitudinally, and two of them\nmade : whereas, if the trunk be of unusual size, four and even five may be cut out\nsimultaneously by splitting. These shields are all cut somewhat after the same\npattern, varying from about 22 to 26 inches in length, 7£ to 9 inches in width, and\nhaving the handle cut into the back (Figs. 373, 377, 378) : the anterior surfaces\nare markedly convex both longitudinally and transversely (Figs. 374, 375), the\ndegree of convexity varying inversely with the width, while the posterior are\nflattened or even slightly concave (Figs. 379, 380). A fluting is to be seen on\nboth sides, though how far this is purposely or accidentally present in the\nLeichhardt-Selwyn and Cloucurry District examples, which in addition bear a\nsuperposed incised pattern, it is impossible to say.\n\nThe superposed pattern in the examples from those two districts consists of\na sort of looped design on both sides, reminding one somewhat when seen at a\ndistance, though the resemblance may perhaps be considered far-fetched, of the\nplaques on a tortoise-shell (Figs. 376, 377), occasionally, and additionally, there\nmay be one or two transverse cuts above and below, while invariably the incisions\nconstituting the design are subsequently filled in with red ochre. In the Upper\nGeorginaand Boulia Districts, the pattern on the front is more complicated (Fig.\n373, 374a.b., 375), a fluting drawn to special design: it might be described as\ncomposed of numerous lines iunning parallel with the two vertical edges of the\nweapon, the two series of curved flutes thus produced crossing in the middle line,\nand forming a more or less concentric shuttle-pattern around the central portion\nof the shield. The pattern on the back may occasionally be similar to the front,\nthough usually it is in the form of parallel longitudinal straight lines. FIGHTING-WEAPONS. 151\n\nenlarged and tapers to a point : a good one is usually incised with some circular\nbands at the handle {see handle-marks in sects. 241, 255), and a longitudinal\nfluting which reaches either to the tip or ceases abruptly about an inch from it.\n\nThe name applied to this weapon in the Boulia District is mor-ro ; the\nMitakoodi call it ma-ro. The nulla-nulla in these districts is not so much a\n\" hand \" instrument as a throwing implement — i.e., it is used more for throwing\nat short distances than for hitting at close quarters.\n\n257. Stone-knives. — The stone-knife consists of a chipped flint-flake blade\nfixed into a rounded or oval handle made of cementing-substance (Figs. 387, 389).\nThe flake, varying from about two to over six inches in length, has from three (Fig.\n388) to five or more facets (Fig. 387), an extra large one, as a rule, forming one\nside of the blade ; the whole knife is known by the same name as the blade. The\ncement-handle is either smoothed nicely off to fit the hollow of the hand, or else\nmay be lengthened by the addition of a piece of wood (Fig. 390) : in the Boulia\nDistrict the handle is spoken of as kun-ti ma-ro— i.e., cement-possessor. Along\nwith the implement there is very often a sort of sheath made of fine strips of\nbark longitudinally placed, wound round and round with opossum-string, and\nenclosing at its apex some emu-feather? which, projecting inwards, protect the\nknife-point (Fig. 386) : at Glenormiston and Boulia this sheath is called the\nmoon-ta-bil-la. The flint stone from which the blade is made is obtainable along\nthe head of the Burke and Wills Rivers, in the Leichhardt-Selwyn and the Toko\nRanges, and Upper Georgina River, but not on the Mulligan. From the\nLeichhardt-Selwyn and Upper Georgina Districts, the stone-knife travels, for\npurposes of exchange and barter — (a) across to the Mitakoodi and Woonamurra,\n(b) to the Middle Diamantina River via Noranside, Boulia, and Marion Downs or\nSpringvale, ((?) to the Upper Diamantina via Kynuna. The names it receives in\nthe various ethnographical districts are to be seen in sect. 55.\n\nThe stone-blade, certainly in the eastern portions of North- West- Central\nQueensland, owing to contact with a higher civilisation, is gradually being\nreplaced by the iron, filed and ground down, obtained from disused shear-blades,\nbarrel-hoops, &c. ; the handle is also similarly undergoing modifications, a pretty\ncommon form being its encasement in the testicle-pouch removed from sheep,\ngoat, or kangaroo.\n\n258. The Stone Tomahawk (Fig. 391) used to be made years ago, previous to\nthe advent of the whites and their more serviceable metal ones, by the Kalkadoon,\nMitakoodi, &c, from a kind of greenstone obtained in the Leichhardt-Selwyn\nEanges. I am informed on very reliable authority that at the present time (1896),\nat a spot called \"Bora,\" in the close neighbourhood of the Bower Bird Gold Field,\non the Upper Leichhardt River, are to be seen remains of one of the pits or\nquarries whence this particular stone was originally obtained. From descriptions\ngiven me by the older blackfellows I find that the stone-head itself used to be cut\nas follows : — A lump about the required size was first of all broken away, and parts\nchipped off here and there with another similar piece of rock until the necessary\nshape would be roughly attained. A whole day perhaps would be. occupied in\ndoing this, while another twenty-four hours would be required for the grinding\ndown, with water, along another smooth piece of the same material until such\ntime as the edge would be sharpened enough for use. Some of these stone-heads\nreach a considerable size, one in my possession, found in the neighbourhood of\nBoulia, measuring over 9 inches in its greatest diameter. It is very rare now-adays to meet with one of these weapons in its entirety. The handles of the few\nin my possession are formed of a single piece of wood, bent at its middle, so as\nto form two limbs which together constitute the handle by being firmly bound\nabove and below with opossum-twine, &c. ; the stone-head is fixed into the wooden\nloop with \" spinifex\" or beef -wood gum. I have not come across any examples\nwhere the stone is fixed into the fork of a limb. The individual will leave camp for three or four days, and subsist only on
bushes, &c. — that is, practically starve himself : he gets more or less " cranky" and

Being with, immense eyes and very big ears, Ten-gul-a-goo-lun, who teaches
