263. Fortunately for himself, however, the patient is not always so weakminded as to give up all hope, but, at length recovering a bit, pulls himself together
and determines upon finding out who it was that had wrought him the injury.
He either asks a friend or relative, who possibly may mention the name of some
poor wretch upon whom he (the friend) may have a " down," or else sees the
imaginary culprit in a dream ; should both these means fail him he consults a
" doctor." These three methods of inquiry have each their separate accompaniments.
In the case where he learns the information required through the agency of a
friend, he seeks the doctor's assistance, and by means of some sort of a present,
such as a blanket, human-hair belt, &c, prevails upon him to " point" the bone
at his alleged assailant (and get some of his blood in retaliation, sect. 264). It
may happen, however, that the alleged culprit is physically more powerful or
possessed of greater personal influence than the medicine-man himself, in which
case the latter may decline the job, being fearful of the retribution that
might follow should his action in the matter be subsequently discovered ; at any
rate, in the long run a willing practitioner is obtained. If in a dream he
recognises his enemy, or the doctor who lent assistance, he will perhaps go and
fight one or both — if he thinks he can do so successfully ; he will not attempt to
do either of them to death, but only just cripple them with knife, spear, or
"boomerang, and take measures in addition to have each of them " pointed " at
"vrith a bone in return. The reason of his not wishing to actually kill
(jne or other is that so long as his own blood remains in the receptacle of the
T)one-apparatus in the alleged enemy's possession, and is not properly rinsed out
"with water (sects. 267, 268), his own life remains in danger.

Where corroborative evidence, by both preceding methods, is wanting, the

injured individual will consult some medical friend of his, and, with the usual gift,

msk him to discover his assailant, and possibly the name of his alleged enemy may

T)e divulged straight away. - More often, however, the doctor is not quite such a

:f ool as to commit himself so readily, but exercises his power of removing from

^within the patient's body the actual bone, pebble, flint, &c, which the would-be

^murderer had invisibly inserted there (sect. 264). Having inquired where the

"bodily pains were most marked, or their effects still remain, he sets about rubbing

or massaging the affected parts, perhaps at intervals rinsing his hands in water.

Be may also blow upon the patient's chest, take some water into his own mouth

and spit it out again, probably to show that nothing is concealed therein, that

there is no deception in fact, and may even apply his lips in the act of suction to

that portion of the patient's anatomy most complained of. At any rate in a short

time he certainly contrives, by a kind of sleight of hand, to get some sort of a

doctor's gew-gaw, some of the stock-in-trade — bone, flint, quartz, &c. (sect. 261) —

one else who may be present, implicitly believes he has managed to draw out from

appearance on these occasions is certainly very puzzling, even to Europeans : at

any rate there it is, and the sick individual is now absolutely cured, though his life

remains in danger, his life's " blood" being in the enemy's bone- receptacle. Now,

the particular gew-gaw thus apparently removed from the person ailing must

have been placed in the part complained of by some other and rival doctor. The

present consultant therefore examines it most carefully and tells the patient to

which member of the profession it belongs— that is, who did the actual mischief ; he

says he will now try and find out which of the victim's enemies instigated the deed,

privately with bis fellow-practitioners, and may suggest some personally obnoxious

individual, but the latter may have some friends at court, and the idea is scouted :

at all events, among themselves collectively in secret conclave they hit upon some

poor wretch of a fellow who has perhaps and probably been lately causing trouble

in the camp, and all agree in making him the scape-goat. The particular person

having been selected, the doctor returns to his quondam patient and divulges the

name of bis enemy : the patient will not, however, fight him yet, not until he has

got his would-be destroyer's life-blood similarly into his own possession (sects. 266,

  "passage_text": "265* In the Boulia District the death-bone is \" pointed\" thus : — If singlehanded, and he knows that he can get to within a short distance of his prey, the\ndoctor fixes fhe cup or receptacle of the bone-apparatus upright into the ground,\nwhile the pointer, resting between the big toe and digit, is directed at the person\nselected, the connecting string being held in the hand, and never by any chance\nallowed to touch the earth (Fig. 393a).\n\nAgain, if single-handed, but the victim, owing to the position of his gundi or\nthe presence of others, cannot be approached at short distance, a longer string is\nused : the receptacle is fixed to a stump or tree, while the pointer, which is held\nin the position of rest upon a forked stick firmly planted into the ground, is directed\nas required (Fig. 393 b).\n\nOf course it is always advisable for the practitioner to work the munguni by himself, but sometimes, if in doubt or unsuccessful, he may call in the assistance ot other\nmedicos : in the former case he can keep the transaction secret between himself and\nhis employer, whereas in the latter the evil business might leak out, the danger of\nsuch a contingency being, however, perhaps counterbalanced by the fact that the\nfull responsibility is now shared with others. Should two of them be working\nthe instrument, one holds the pointer and the otfrer the receptacle. When three,\nfour, or even perhaps five medicine- men are pointing 'the bone-apparatus, one\nholds the pointer, another the receptacle, while the remainder support the connecting-string, which under these circumstances would be very much longer than\nthe ordinary. Among those holding the string there may be some intimate friend\nof 'the proposed victim, and he, by means of a secreted flint, &c, may cut the\ntwine while the performance is proceeding : if, on re-tying the string, it again\nbreaks (i.e., is more probably purposely cut), the intended victim is spared.\nThough the others may have a shrewd suspicion as to which of their mates severed\nthe cord, they find it wiser not to express any opinion publicly: they only recognise\nthe fact that whoever did it was afraid of stating his convictions openly\nwhen the secret conclave (sect. 263) was held. Under such circumstances the\ndoctor returns* to his employer and explains how it was that his endeavours to\nobtain the required blood, &c, were unsuccessful: the employer can please\nhimself whether he consults another medical man or not.\n\nIn the Cloncurry District, the manner in which the munguni is pointed by\nthe Mitakoodi doctor is almost identical, both in procedure and results, with the\nmethod holding good in the Boulia District. The receptacle is clutched between\nthe two knees, the string held in the hand, while the pointer, directed in the\nproper quarter, is made to rest upon a branch or stick in the manner indicated in\nFig. 394. In low tones, so as not to notify his presence, he sings a dirge (the\nmeaning of which he does not know) while pointing.\n\nIn the Upper Georgina District, the traditions of the bone-apparatus are\nupheld, with more or less variations, both among the Undekerebina and Yaroinga\ntribes. In addition to \" pointing\" by the ordinary method, the Yaroinga doctor\n\" shoots\" the pointer with a sharp push from the open palm of one hand along\nthe prongs of a forked stick held in the other into the required direction (Fig. 896),\nhis assistant, who has hold of the connecting-string, pulling the pointer back\nagain as it falls : this procedure may be repeated a few times.\n\nIn the Leichhardt-Selwyn District, the Kalkadoon doctor usually employs\nanother to help him \" point,\" the one holding the pointer and the other the\nreceptacle."
}

HaviDg by some one or oilier of the above methods of \" pointing\"\nobtained the required blood (sect. 264) in the receptacle of the \"bone-apparatus\"\nthe doctor puts into it the pointer, tip downwards, around the exposed butt-end of\nwhich and the otherwise open mouth of the cylinder he fixes a lot of the usual\ncementing substance so as to completely seal it : outside the whole concern he\nwinds the connecting-string round and round. Though he will swear to his\nemployer as to the presence and genuineness of the contained blood, it is difficult\nto learn whether the medical man has inserted some of his own, or that of some\nanimal,- or indeed any at all : he naturally takes every precaution, to maintain the\ndeception, that no one shall actually see what he does enclose in the cylinder\nwhen sealing it. But the employer wants to make doubly sure that he really\nhas the blood of his alleged would-be destroyer, and not that of someone else who\nmay have been u pointed \" at in mistake. He therefore, in company with the\ndoctor who procured it, will in a few days' time, to avert suspicion, leave the\ncamp after dark, and in some sequestered spot kindle a fire, over which they warm\nthe bone-apparatus with its ghostly contents. Leaving the medicine-man to keep\ncratch, he returns to camp, divulges his mission to no one, but enters into conversation with his alleged assailant on any ordinary everyday topic, watches most\ncarefully to see if he is at all sick or not, and may casually get him to admit that\nlie is feeling a bit tired or is a little out of sorts. This admission, simple as it is,\nconstitutes ample proof of guilt under the circumstances, but the avenger says\nxi o thing, continues the conversation to allay even the slightest suspicion, parts\nAvith him on apparently friendly terms, and sneaks back to the doctor, to whom he\nnarrates exactly what has taken place. Supposing that the wrong individual blood\nlias been \" caught,\" i.e., an innocent person has been \" pointed\" at in mistake — and\n~fchis is judged to be the ca»e when not the slightest sign of sickness is discoverable —\n\"the medicine-man breaks open the top of the receptacle, which he rinses out and\n^washes well in water, so as to allow of its being used again in another attempt.\n\n267. But if everything is satisfactory, and the blood of the required culprit\nlas been really (as is believed) obtained, the one in possession has only to warm\n\"the apparatus again over the fire to make his alleged, and now proven, enemy\nmore sick ; to destroy it in the flames to make him actually die ; or to rinse it in\nwater and rub fat of any description over it to put him all to rights again. He\nthus has his enemy completely in his power, and continues to make him sick —\nthere is generally some ague, venereal, or chronic rheumatism, &c., about — but\nwill not kill him — i.e., burn the munguni — for fear of his own life, which continues\nin danger so long as his own blood (which can be affected, for good or for evil,\nand by similar methods) remains in his enemy's possession.\n\n268. After a longer or shorter interval, when the passions have subsided — and\nTime heals all things, even the quarrels of the aboriginal — the complainant will\nconsider that he has punished his enemy sufficiently by making him so seriously\nill. He will find some opportunity for making an explanation, and admit, more or\nless truly, that it was he,* but only in retaliation, who \" caught \" and still possesses\nhis blood : the owner of the latter will naturally, and most conscientiously, of\ncourse, deny the charge in toio at first, but when the strong array of facts is\nmarshalled before him, admit it for peace and security sake, and invent or find\nperhaps some trifling excuse to justify his alleged original act of injury. They do\nnot fight, being mutually afraid of each other, now that each is firmly believed to be\nin possession of the other's \" blood,\" but settle the matter amicably, the mutual\nunderstanding being cemented by the alleged careful washing out and rinsing of\nthe respective mungunis, one of which — the original alleged enemy's — is probably,\nand, of course, in most cases, not really existent.\n\n269. Death from Snake-bite. — To account for a death from snake-bite — which\napparently only rarely happens, and in such cases the purely natural cause and\nfatal effect are not reconciled — a variation in the superstition of the death-bone\nis brought into requisition. This modification in the procedure, though known\nthroughout the whole Boulia District, is said to be only occasionally employed.\nBy means similar to those already mentioned, proof is forthcoming that the\nreceptacle of the bone-apparatus actually contains the particular person's blood\n\n158 DISEASE, ACCIDENT, DEATH. CANNIBALISM."

The latter may depart as usual on some hunting expedition, and become fully occupied in the excitement of the chase, when he\nsuddenly feels something at his leg or foot, and sees a snake just in the act of\nbiting him. Strange to say, this particular kind of snake will now immediately\ndisappear : it does not crawl into the ground, or hide under a stone like any\nordinary ophidian would do, but actually vanishes away into space. Indeed, by\nthis very process of invisibility the person bitten recognises that some enemy has\nbeen \" pointing \" at him the munguni, and that through this particular form of it\nhe is sure to die ; nothing can possibly save him. He makes no effort, in fact, to\napply a remedy, loses heart, gives way and dies (see treatment of ordinary, i.e.,\nnon-fatal snake-bite, sect. 280). Supposing the gin of the thus snake-bitten\nindividual to be present at the time of the occurrence, she will run back to camp\nas fast as she can go and tell one of the doctors. The latter, from a careful crossexamination as to the nature of the bite, the variety of the snake, and the\ncondition of the patient, will soon gather all the information he requires, and then\nglance up at the skies to see if Mulkari is spitting or not : if, as he says, he does\nnot recognise this supernatural Being expectorating from above, he tells her that\nsome mortal must have got her husband's blood, using this particular form of the\nmunguni to effect his purpose, and that it is impossible to save his iife. Furthermore, at some future time, the doctor referred to will tell her who actually did\nthe mischief : the widow will not learn this information perhaps for some months\nto come, but when she does she will tell her brothers and other kindred, who then\ntake the necessary steps to avenge her husband's death.\n\n270. Other Diseases and Accidents produced by the Death-bone. — Instead of\ninserting a snake in the death-bone receptacle with the required blood, certain\ndoctors, and they only, can talk to the captured blood and tell it to kill the person\nfrom whom it has been taken, by lightning, by the fall of a tree, or to injure him\nby running a thorn into his foot, or inflicting upon him some vile complaint or\ndisease.\n\nAt Bedouri, on the southern confines of the Boulia District, among the\nOoioopooloo tribe, still another modification of the munguni is the wul-loo-ka,\nwhich is believed to be similar in mode and action, but can be used between very\nlong distances. Thus, one of the Bedouri men may have a grudge against a\nBoulia black, and will tell a white or a blue crane, or even a pelican, to travel all\nover the intervening distance, and by \" pointing \" get the blood for him. Some time\nafter, during the shades of night, the victim sees one of these birds in question and\nwill throw a stick at it to drive it away, but the creature, being engaged in\n\"pointing,\" will not budge for some little time; it will only fly away back to Bedouri\nwhen it has got a sufficient quantity of blood in the bone-apparatus receptacle.\nTo make sure now that he really has possession of his victim's blood, the would-be\nassailant at Bedouri will send four or five other birds again to Boulia in order to\nglean the necessary information as to whether the individual upon whom he has\nsinister designs is sick or not : he is afraid to send the same bird by itself on the\nsecond journey in case it were to \" gammon \" him. This procedure is considered\nto be far more potent in its action than the ordinary form of munguni. Indeed,\nMulkari invented this method originally, though he taught both systems to the\nOoioopooloo men, whence the commoner process travelled all over the district :\nthe secret of the wul-loo-Jca, however, they have kept to themselves, and will on\nno account teach the details of the process to their northern neighbours.\n\n271. Women Doctors. — Though a woman dare not handle or look upon a\nmunguni, she sometimes knows and practises the \" trick \" of removing by mouth\nor hand (sect. 263) the particular gew-gaw which is alleged and believed to have\nbeen inserted, and to be prolonging the sickness, in the patient's body. She may\nherself be a doctor's wife or not, but on no account is she ostensibly allowed to\njoin in the secret deliberations of the other medical practitioners. It she herself\nwishes to get possession of another woman's blood, she may prevail, if married,\nupon her husband, or, if single, upon her brother, to put her wishes into practical\nexecution."
}

The Pearl-plate, like the death-bone, is made to account for various\nforms of sickness and death, which otherwise to the aboriginal mind would be\ninexplicable. It consists of a flat, more or less, triangular piece of pearl-shell,\nwith rounded angles, measuring in its greatest length, from middle of base to the\nsubtended angle, at which some cementing substance with a piece of hair-twine is\nattached, from 1£ ^° 2 inches (Fig. 396). Brought by the Workia tribes into\nNorth- West-Central Queensland to Lake Nash and neighbourhood, it reaches\non the one hand the Leichhardt-Selwyu, and en the other the Upper Georgina\nDistrict. The Kalkadoon, who call this implement the che-ka-la-ri (cf. sect. 184),\nemploy it far more frequently perhaps than the munguni, and have introduced it\namong the Mitakoodi, who now practice it with the same evil intent. Through\nthe Yaroinga, by whom it is named ker-ka-la, the Undekerebina tribe of the\nToko Ranges has also come to learn its uses. The usual precedure is for the\nassailant to come, ordinarily at night-time, as close as possible to his intended\nand unconscious victim, to hold the implement by the cemented corner at arm'slength, and, through the air in the direction indicated, make two horizontal and two\nvertical passes : the former is considered symbolical of the cutting of the throat,\nthe latter the ripping-up of the belly-wall. The Undekerebina, who apparently\nattach great importance to this particular mode of injury, take extra precautions\nlest any innocent or harmless person be hurt by the too great extent of the\nhorizontal sweep, and will therefore hold up the other fore-arm (Fig. 397) to\nlimit it : or, again, with a similar object in view, the performer will open his legs,\ntuck his head well down, and then put the pearl-shell into execution (Fig. 398),\nthe lower limbs limiting the movement either to the right or to the left.\n\n• 273. The Death-powder. — The Workia people, it would seem, are also\nresponsible for the death-powder, the mo-a-ri or moy-a-ri, somewhat of the appearance of very white ashes which, placed anywhere in close proximity to where the\nvictim is sleeping, under his blanket, &c, will kill him in no time. This practice\nprevails among the Yaroinga and the Kalkadoon : through the latter it has reached\nthe Mitakoodi on the one hand and the Yellunga of Noranside on the other.\nIn the Boulia District, Noranside is the only locality where it has been noted : the\nsuperstition is certainly not met with at Boulia. The Mitakoodi speak of the\npowder as the mou-ar, and so that the performer should not injure himself by\ncontact he sprinkles it where required from out of a mussel -shell : the same tribe\nalso use a reddish powder, mung-gil-li, with similar methods and design, but the\nexact composition of either material, which unfortunately I was never allowed to\nsee, is unknown to me. In the neighbourhood of Normanton, outside this\ndistrict, a specimen of this powder was found to be ground glass. There is\nsuspicion that this particular superstition has its origin in the fact that in the\nstores on all these Western stations the large quantity of strychnine, the poisonous\nproperties of which many of these aboriginals fully appreciate, is always coloured\nwith ruddle — i.e., red ochre — to minimise the chances of accident.\n\n274. The Bone-pin or chi-roo-ko (in the Pitta- Pitta language) is another instrument, perhaps a development of the munguni \" pointer,\" brought into requisition for\nproducing venereal and other cognate disorders, fatal or not, which otherwise are\ninexplicable : the aboriginal has not yet learnt that these particular diseases are\ncapable of transmission by sexual connection. Besides being used in the Boulia\nDistrict, the chi-roo-ko is at present employed by the Yaroinga in the Upper\nGeorgina, and by the Kalkadoon in the Lichhardt-Selwyn District, though I have\nonly Pitta- Pitta corroborative evidence for the latter statement : a slight variation\nof it is certainly in vogue among the Mitakoodi of the Cloncurry District under\nthe name of je-go. In its ordinary form, the chi-roo-ko consists of a short emuhone from 2 to 2£ inches long, filed to a point — a small edition of the munguni\n\"pointer\" — or perhaps the beak of some long-necked diver-bird, having a little\nspinif ex-gum attached to the base (Fig. 399). There are two methods adopted\nin its employment. If placed underground with the point up, but not visible, in\nthe situation where the victim has been expelling one or other of the products of\nthe emunctories, he or she develops some form of venereal disease, and subsequent\nrotting-away of the privates : if similarly placed in the gundi, or wherever else he\n\n160 DISEASE, ACCIDENT, DEATH. CANITCBALISM.\n\nor sbe may be sleeping, it may cause such a disturbance of the general health as\nto result even in death. The J&itakoodi make their je-go from a human arm-bone :\nit is of about the same size as the chi-rooJco, but with beef -wood gum at the blunt\nextremity, and when in use is hidden anywhere underneath where the victim may\nbe sleeping. Both chi-roo-ko and je-go can be used by the medical as well as the\nlay fraternity, but never by women. In all cases, the assailant may be discovered\nas with the munauni, either by consulting a doctor or by revelation in a dream,\nsubsequent retaliation being effected by similar means : as soon as the implement\nis removed from out of the ground, the sick individual makes a speedy recovery."

  "passage_text": "275. Incurable Blindness. — The development of blindness, when not explicable\nby visible traumatic causes, is in the case of men accounted as a punishment, by\nhuman agency, for a continued persistency in \" catching\" — i.e. 9 raping — married\nwomen when alone and unprotected out in the bush. In the Boulia District, this\npunishment of blindness or me-puk-koo-re-a (cf. Pitta-Pitta me, an eye, puk-ha-,\nto cut, Ac.) can be inflicted by anyone except a woman. The individual whose\nhonour has been sullied gets two of the incisor teeth of a young opossum and ties\nthem with twine, derived from the same animal, one to each of his little fingers,\non their inner aspects. So prepared, he comes into camp and squats down with\nthe chin resting on his closed hands (Pig. 400), taking up # such position that he\ncan get a good view of the delinquent without exciting suspicion. He watches\nhis opportunity to get into line with the offender's eyes, and, without being noticed\nof course, stretches forwards in required direction with both hands, one on a higher\nlevel than the other, and with the little fingers (all the other digits remaining\nclosed) claws into the air at one eye (Fig. 401) : after a few seconds' interval\nhe shifts the position of his hands, the one which was on a higher level before\nbeing now lower, and \" makes for\" the other eye with a similar clawing. After use,\nthe opossum teeth and string are destroyed by fire. The result is that, although\nthe culprit is totally unconscious of what has been done to his visual organs, his.\neye-sight becomes subsequently affected, he gets quite and incurably blind, and\ncan see no more women to assault.\n\nIn the Cloncurry District, when the Mitakoodi want to \" blind \" a man, they\ndo it by \" singing \" only, casting over him a sort of spell, as it were.\n\n276. Drowning. — Death by drowning is a phenomenon explained, in the entire\nBoulia District at least, by means of Kanmare, the huge supernatural water- snake\nalready mentioned (sect. 260). For instance, when about to swim across any big\nstream or river that he suspects or fears, the aboriginal will speak to this Being,\nand express himself somewhat as follows : — \" Do not touch me. I belong to this\ncountry.\" But were he to cross even his own country's river with a stranger to\nthe district, it is possible that; he might be engulfed. Again, whenever a big flood\ncomes up, it brings Kanmare in its wake, so that, supposing our traveller wants to\neffect a crossing, he will only venture in up to bis waist : if the water be too warm\nhe will get across either there or at some other spot ; but if too cold, and he\npersists in the attempt, he is sure to be caught by Kenmare — i.e., drowned.\nNothing can cure him or bring back animation.\n\n277. Sudden Disappearance. — In the Cloncurry District any sudden disappearance (what Europeans would probably speak of as murder and concealment of\nthe body) is credited to Mo-ki-pi-ung-o. This individual, this \" bogie-man,\" who\nlives underground in the seclusion of the mountain fastnesses, is somewhat like a\nblackfellow in appearance, but has some very long teeth with which he can easily\nbite through a man's neck : he drags his victim into the \" pit,\" where he finishes\nby making a meal off him.\n\n278. individual always to remain good, he would, barring the munguni, and " accident"
of death by actual physical violence — e.g., spear, boomerang, &c— probably live for
ever. It is only a child that can die " by itself." In his natural state, the fear
of death is but as nothing to the savage ; he has a hazy notion of the corpse
"getting older and moving about elsewhere," when he ceases to bring food and
tobacco any longer to the burial-place (sects. 280, 291): he has no dread of
future punishment, no hope of reward in another life. Among the Boulia
natives, with whom I could converse in their own language, I am absolutely
convinced that their belief concerning a future state is as represented : in other
districts, when conversing on these topics, interpreters had of course to be made
use of.

280. Treatment of Non-fetal Snake-bite. — I will now consider the various

ailments or accidents, temporary in their nature, and trivial in their results,

which to the aboriginal mind are considered as arising from simple every-day

causes — i.e., which have been induced without the intervention of the munguni,

and are amenable to ordinary simple treatment. The most interesting of these is

non-fatal snake-bite, the treatment of which in the Boulia District should be

compared with the munguni variety of snake-bite (sect. 269) that invariably ends

in the death of the person attacked. In this case, the sufferer would see the

creature gliding away after it had bitten him, and would carefully watch the hole

into which it hides : this he immediately blocks up, and makes a careful note of

±he exact spot. With his hair-belt, or any other convenient twine, he next ties two

Xigatures around the limb bitten, above and below the knee if on the leg, or above

«nd below the elbow if on the hand, " to stop the blood come up ": if possible, he

»pplies suction to the wound. His gin, or any other mate who may be present,

"would rush back to consult the nearest doctor, and returning, dig a largish hole in

(5lo8e proximity to where the accident took place, kindle a fire in it and heat some big

stones and lumps of rock : when these have become sufficiently hot and the flames

somewhat subsident, a lot of fresh leafy boughs and branches and leaves, sprinkled

with water to prevent ignition, are placed on top. Upon this smoking mass of foliage

"the bitten individual now lies, and what with the smouldering embers and hot steam

arising from the leaves he soon becomes enveloped in perspiration, falls asleep for

two or three hours, wakes up refreshed, has a "spit," and is quite recovered. In

the meantime, however, the medicine-man has not been idle, for he of course has

had a share in the cure : when the messenger first came to report the accident, he

would, after cross-examination, look up at the sky aud declare that he could see

Mulkari spitting, and that therefore the patient would be all right if he went

under the prescribed treatment. Furthermore, the doctor himself comes to the

place where the accident happened, is shown the identical spot where the snake

lies imprisoned, digs it out, and lets it travel away a few feet before commencing

to pelt at it with stones. During this process the snake gradually becomes

smaller and smaller until, from &n original length of 3 or 4 feet, it may dwindle

down to, 12 or 10 inches : the creature, thus rendered harmless, is carried back ta)

camp, where the medicine- man, turning its skin half-way inside out while still

alive, throws it into the water, and so makes an end of it. It is needless to say

that no lay-man is allowed to witness the process of causing the ophidian to

diminish in size. The blacks will admit that if an infant or young child is bitten

by a snake it cannot usually be cured unless all the above performances are

quickly gone through : if, for instance, the accident takes place three or four

miles from camp, the little sufferer cannot possibly stand the delay like an elderly

individual would. Among the Mitak^odi the treatment of ordinary snake-bite is

very similar, but no • " tricks " on the part of the doctor are brought into

requisition : suction, with or without scarifying by knife or stone, and ligature,

followed by sweating over heated leaves, especially if the particular species is

believed to be a dangerous one.

281. Fractures. — "With regard to fractured limbs, two to four sticks in the
rough may be tied on a broken arm or leg, and left there perhaps for from one to
two months : the value of the remedy is rendered inactive, however, by the ftcfc
that these splints are not of sufficient length to keep the adjacent joints at rest.
At other times (e.g., among the Mitakoodi), instead of splints, the limb may be

162 DISEASE, ACCIDENT, DEATH. CANNIBALISM.

wrapped up in opossum skins, and tied tightly round and round with twine. The
value of slings, crutches, &c, in these cases is unknown : if an arm is broken, it
is supported by the hand of the opposite one ; if a leg, the patient is carried to
camp and laid there, &c.

282. The various Chants and Dirges for exorcising Ailments, inducing Sleep, ftc,
have been so handed down from one to another, both individually and tribally,
that though some of the lay as well as the professional members of the
community know several of them by rote, none of them understand their actual
meaning : for instance, here is one used at Boulia, in addition to other remedies,
for dispelling stomach-ache and diarrhoea — " koo-n&w-bi ma-r8-£Z-yi la~rd-0(roy-k&
wt^-pS-di," where the root koo-na (i.e., faeces) is the only syllable intelligible
to me. It must not be forgotten that chants and dirges may, on the other hand,
be utilised for producing sickness, &c."

  "passage_text": "283. Smearing of Blood, of Perspiration; Drinking of Blood, of Seminal Fluid ;\nWet-cupping. — Human blood is used for smearing all over the body, trunk, limbs,\nand face, in various obscure affections, and internal pains of one sort and another.\nIn the Boulia District this smearing of blood is Known as gim-ha-lo-weon-di-a\n{gim-ba^kim-ba = blood, -lo = prepositional suffix by, with, [sect. 24],tc = euphonic,\noon-da- = to grease or smear). The blood itself is removed from any other\napparently healthy individual, but never a woman, in one or other of the two\nfollowing methods : — With a string or other ligature tied tightly round and above\nthe main prominence of the biceps muscle, the elbow is either strongly flexed\n(Fig. 402a), or while made to press upon something behind (Fig. 402 b) equally\nstrongly extended : in the former case, the incision with the stone knife, &c, into\nthe posterior ulnar vein (the blood-vessel ordinarily employed) can be made by the\nindividual himself, in the latter by some other person. The blood is collected into\na koolamon, and the wound, dressed with fat, bound round with a leaf or two.\nBy means of a bundle of emu feathers the blood so obtained is dabbed all over the\npatient from head to heels, while his gin or some male friend, more usually the\nformer, rubs it in with the flat of the hands, the massage, such as it is, lasting\noften well over a quarter of an hour : in addition to the external application of the\nremedy, the patient may drink some or even all of it, in the latter case postponing\nthe \" rubbing\" portion of the treatment for a subsequent occasion. This bloodsmearing cure is in vogue throughout North-West-Central Queensland. The\nKalkadoon, in addition, apply a method, without rubbing, wherein the whole body,\nhead included, is covered with red ochre. Sweat removed from under the armpits,\nand sm eared in a similar manner as the blood, is also believed to have wonderful\ncurative powers, especially in extremity throughout all these districts. The\ndrinking of seminal fluid in cases of sickness will be referred to in the ethnopornographical chapter (sect. 305). Wet-cupping, by means of superficial\nincisions made by stone-knives, &c, is not infrequently practised over an inflamed\nand painful knee or shoulder-joint.\n\n284. Smearing of Fat. —Iguana-, snake-, or any other kind of fat or grease,\nmixed more or less with mud and dirt, is used as a dressing for cuts and wounds\nof all description, the latter never been allowed to heal by \" first intention\" : this\ncustom of greasing an incision is very common everywhere. A clean-cut incised\nwound is called in the Pitta- Pitta language koo-re-a, while any open or punctured\none, due to a boomerang or spear, is named wil-pa. Fat may also be employed\nas a liniment for rubbing over tired or aching limbs, and in such circumstances\naffords apparently speedy relief. Independently of sickness, the greasing of the\nbodies of children and infants is referred to in sect. 328,\n\n285. Poultices. — The only application of a poultice that has come under\nobservation is the practice prevailing among the Mitakoodi for the cure of a bad\nheadache : some box-tree bark, subsequently to having been hammered and\npounded, is soaked in hot water, and the mass so produced held with a piece of\nbark, cloth, &c, by the hand — not tied — to the particular part affected. On other\noccasions, in the same tribe, a bundle of heated fresh leaves may be tied on to the\nforehead for a similar purpose."
}

Amulets and Charms. — The min-ma, min-ta-ra, or mul-ta-ra consists of\na bundle of emu feathers, either tied up loosely with opossum-string or enclosed\nin a curved spindle-shaped net (Pig. 403) tied on anywhere where pain may be ;\nfor instance, over the forehead for headache (Pitta- Pitta, ka-ti-pul-ka-le-a — see\nVocabulary, sect. 44), over the belly for stomach-ache (Pitta-Pitta, um-ba put-ya\nput-ya mul-le-a, tool-chi koon-di koon-di, &c. — see Vocabulary, sect. 44) . This charm\nis met with in the Boulia and Leichhardt-Selwyn Districts.\n\nA rather rare amulet, the rnun-da-koo-e-a, is of a flattened-spindle form, about\n& or 6 inches long, made of emu feathers, which, after been placed lengthways and\nImndlewise are wound round and round with opossum- string, and then coated all\nover with red-ochre grease : a slender piece of bone of some sort is occasionally\nenclosed in its centre. Originally, in the olden days, this was used as a sign of\ngood faith to be forwarded to some other friendly tribe whose assistance was\nrequired in fighting a common enemy : in those times there was but one of them\nin each camp, and the privileged individual used to wear it on his chest, on\nwhich it would hang by means of a string passing round the neck. Subsequently\nthis mundakooea came to have remedial properties attributed to it, and, worn in\nthe similar position, has been gradually imitated and supplanted by the more\ncommon wor-a-ka. [Compare notes on death and burial (sect. 291) for the use\nof the mundakooea among the Mitakoodi.] The woraka (Pig. 404) is a similar\nimplement to the preceding, but usually more rounded, and so may be described\nalmost as cigar-shaped : it may also be painted as before, entirely red, or in transverse band 8 of alternately red and yellow colours. Worn over the chest it is\nused to relieve obscure pains, a troubling cough, &c, and, as a survival, may still\nbe utilised for -collecting aid -in case of warfare. The woraka, its Boulia District\nname, is known as u-la-ri by the Kalkadoon, who also manufacture it ; indeed, it\nis believed to have been introduced originally to the latter by their northern\nneighbours, the Workia.\n\n287. Medicinal Plants. — The gum (Pitta- Pitta, ko-ka) of the blood-wood tree\n• (Pitta-Pitta, re-chin-di) is used both as a local and internal application for venereal\n\nsores : in the former case it is used as powder and dusted on, in the latter it is\nboiled with water. This remedy is used on the Upper Georgina, and in the\nCloncurry, Leichhardt-Selwyn, and Boulia Districts.\n\nA species of \" penny-royal \" (Pitta-Pitta, po-kan-gud-ye) is drunk in the form\nof a decoction, like tea, with apparently very beneficial results, in coughs or colds\n(Pitta-Pitta, ka-rin-ga~ri) : a very common remedy in the Boulia and Leichhardt-\nSelwyn Districts.\n\nIn the country of the Mitakoodi, the u-ka-ta, a species of rosella growing on\nthe mountains, is also made a decoction of for the same purpose.\n\nSimilarly strongly-scented plants are used everywhere for \" sniffing at \" in\ncases of headache.\n\nThe belief is pretty common that any sort of grass or shrub growing near the\nwater's edge will relieve difficult or painful micturition : various species of\nEuphorbia are the plants very frequently used for this purpose.\n\n288. The actual spot being now determined upon, some set about digging a grave, while others assist in cutting logs\nand sticks from 3 to 6 feet long. The depth of the grave appears to vary with\nthe nature of the soil, but about 4 feet is a fair average, though this is\noften greater. When all is ready, the body is laid in horizontally, face up, with\nthe head pointing in the direction of the north : this is considered to be the\northodox \" good-fellow\" direction in which the body ought to lie, but too many\ndie nowadays, and the survivors appear too lazy to trouble themselves concerning\nsuch details. Some of the longer logs cover the body in, then a layer or two of\nshorter ones are placed transversely, and next comes the filling up with earth : on\ntop of all this are placed logs and bushes, perhaps some heavy stones, all closely\ninterlaced, and reaching to a height of from 3 to 4 feet above the adjacent\nsurface, which is cleared and cleaned to a distance of a few feet all the way round\n(Fig 405). The reason given for the fixing of the logs, &c, is to prevent the\ncorpse from being dug up and tampered with by the dingoes, while the explanation of the cleaned space is the prevention of the timber igniting in case of a\nbush-fire. The various goods belonging to the deceased — boomerangs, spears. &c. —\nare either buried with him, destroyed bv fire, or sometimes, though rarely, distributed\namong his \"brothers,\" but never his children. Furthermore, his personal individual\nname (autonym) dies with him, never to be again mentioned, a custom especially\nmarked in the case of near relatives, who do not care to be reminded of the event :\nit was mainly owing to this circumstance that attempts at forming reliable conclusions as to possible connections between personal individual names proved to\nbe fruitless (sect. 67). Burial follows almost immediately upon death taking\nplace, though if the closing scene occurs at night it is not carried out until early\ndawn. The corpse itself is in no ways decorated or painted.\n\nAt the grave, and while it is being dug, in the midst of the wailing and the\nweeping, the women will cut themselves with stone or glass down the outer and\nanterior aspects of the thighs, in numerous more or less parallel superficial\nincisions. In the neighbourhood of Glenormiston the women, previous to the\ncutting, have been known to wash their thighs with their own urine collected in the\nhands. These signs of grief with the females have their counterpart among the\nmales at Carlo, Glenormiston, Herbert Downs, and Roxburgh, but apparently not\nat Boulia, who make a single large and much deeper crucial incision on the\ncorresponding portion of the thigh : in the old days, before the advent of the\nwhites, deaths were of infinitely less frequent occurrence than now, with the\nresult that the old practice of a u cross\" for each adult male deceased would now\nbe impossible. Occasionally among the elder men one or two of these crucial\nincisions are still to be observed.\n\nThe actual burial being completed, they all return home with many a sob and\ntear, and plaster their heads with blobs of pa-fa or \" kopi,\" a sort of gypsum,\nthese lumps at a distance making the whole hair appear one mass of white. In\nany camp uncontaminated and away from the settlements, this plastering is\nadopted by all, no mattef whether the deceased be man, woman, or child,\nthough, as might have been expected, it is worn longer by some than by others,\neven up to six months sometimes in the case of gins mourning their husbands.\nOwing to this fixing up of the hair a mourner is spoken of as pata-maro\n— i.e., plaster-possessor. In addition, the nearer relatives, and they only, colourgrease themselves down as far as to the waist, after the patterns for male\nand female respectively in Figs 407a.b. These nearer relatives, in the\ncase of an adult male, are considered to be the wife, and his brothers and\nsisters by the same mother — not his father or mother : with an adult woman,\nonly the brothers and sisters by the same mother, her husband contenting\nhimself with the plastering. In the case of a young child, no painting would be\nadopted by anyone. So far as the pattern is concerned, the yellow grease is first\nof all smeared over by itself, the design being worked by a scraping off with the\nthree or four clawed finger-tips like the teeth of a comb (cf. sect. 185) : the red is\nput on subsequently, and the design on both back and front is similar. in addition to the " kopi," or more usually when its supply runs short, greased
ashes, or mud by itself, may be smeared over the whole body as external emblems
of grief.

Crying and weeping, but no singing, is repeated nightly for a week or so, up
to a fortnight perhaps, especially by the nearer relatives, who may repair to the
grave for the purpose, the sisters continuing when the brothers cease : they
generally go in parties to the burial-place, being afraid to go singly on account of
seeing the deceased's Moma (sect. 260) passibly. Tobacco, matches, food, pituri,
a pipe, &c, may be left each night at the grave-side, and the individual departed
openly informed to that effect.

When an adult male dies in the Pitta-Pitta country, all his brothers and
sisters are called mun-na moor-ra, a term literally signifying " no-good sticks,"
applied probably in reference to the logs lying upon the deceased's grave : his
wife, a widow, is henceforth known as ka-ri-ou-o, and she remains one for a
twelvemonth or more, until such time as another husband can be found for her.

290. (b) Of a Murderer. — When an individual has been killed by the whole tribe

collectively — that is to say, in punishment for some serious crime — he is usually

made to dig his own grave, which is subsequently closed in similar manner, except

that boomerangs are substituted for the long logs immediately covering the corpse.

Where, as in cases of murder, the assassin has been caught red-handed, the slayer

and slain are buried together in the same grave, previously dug by the survivor

after the customary method. In times of open hostilities, those who are killed

are left on the field by their enemies, with broken spear or boomerang close

beside to show the passing wayfarer how the individuals in question met their

death. In the Pitta- Pitta language a grave is called moorra-kumbo (= stick-stone),

a corpse koon-ta, and the act of dying, to die (also = to lie down), e-che-.

291. (c) In the Cloncurry District. — In the Cloncurry District, among the

IVIitakoodi, the corpse, pa-ra-go (the same name applied to a white man) is buried

usually in a crouching position with head down, enclosed in a net perhaps, then

covered with some ti-tree bark, and the earth thrown on top : no logs or sticks

are piled up above, but the ground is smoothed to the level of the surrounding

surface and a more or less circular area cleaned up. When night falls, a fire is

lighted at a few yards' distance from the grave, and some meat, &c, hung up on

a neighbouring tree : this may be repeated for three or four nights following,

and occasionally now and again during the next few months, until it is believed in

fact that the deceased "has got too old, has gone away somewhere else." In the

olden days the women used to wear the gypsum as a sign of mourning, but

nowadays both sexes only besmear themselves with mud, or else paint themselves

red as far down as the waist : incisions used also to be made along the fronts of the

thighs, several small superficial ones on the women, and two or three deep ones on

the men. Where no visible or otherwise intelligible cause of death presents

itself, one of the doctors will find out whether this is due to Mulkari or his

counterpart who, in the Mitakoodi country, is believed to kill blacks, or to some

human enemy with the munguni : in the latter case he would make-believe that

he had picked up the particular incriminating gew-gaw in the neighbourhood

of the grave, and accuse some individual of having committed the crime. In

other cases, the near relatives of the deceased may learn something for themselves,

by sticking upright a small forked stick on the grave itself, and on it placing a

mundakooea (sect. 286) : this is done at night, and if on the following morning

the mundakooea is found on the ground, it is proof positive that the late lamented

met his death at the hands of an enemy " from a long way country."

292. (n) In the Upper Georgina District, along the river, from Carandotta
upwards, tree-burial is practised. A eort of horizontal platform of logs is
built in the tree about 10 or 12 feet from the ground, and upon this, wrapped
in its net, &c, the corpse is laid : various sticks and bushes are placed on top,
and in and among them the deceased's possessions may bo enclosed. Fig.
406 represents a tree-grave which I found a little beyond Roxburgh : the
body, that of an old Headingly or Carandotta boy, was lying with head to

north-east and feet to south-west. Among the Yaroinga I am informed by
members of the tribe that, in special cases of important personages, when all
the flesh has rotted off, the bones' are subsequently removed and buried in the
ground, with nothing on the surface to indicate their presence beneath.
Gypsum is also used as a sign of mourning : the same custom prevails also in
the Leichhardt-Selwyn District, though the Kalkadoons use red and yellow paint
in addition."

Cannibalism. — Though the primd facie evidence of the practice of\ncannibalism is very meagre, and any information concerning particulars is but\ncharily given by the aboriginals, there is no doubt but that this custon, though\ngradually becoming more and more obsolete, certainly does take jpkce within\ncertain limitations throughout North-West-Central Queensland. Thus in the\nBoulia district, especially with children who die suddenly from no lingering\nillness, portions of the corpse may be eaten by the parents and by their blood\nbrothers and sisters only : the reason assigned is that \" putting them along\nhole\" would make them think too much about their beloved little ones,\nthough unfortunately this is apparently contradicted by the fact that if the\nchild has been ailing a long lime previously and become emaciated, &c,\nit will be buried. Proofs also are to hand that within the last ten years,\nsince 1885, true-blooded aboiiginal children have been killed, with the object\nof being eaten, at Noranside, Eoxburgh, and Carandotta. In the more northern\nareas half-caste infants are not uncommonly murdered at the present time,\neither at the instigation of their white fathers or their assumed black-blooded\nones : but to what extent, in the latter case, for the main purpose of providing\nfood, it is impossible to speak with certainty. My friend Mr. Edwards, late of\nEoxburgh, is the only European who to my knowledge has been an eye-witness of\nsuch an orgie : this was in 1888, between Eoxburgh and Carandotta, when he saw\nan infant being roasted in one of the native ovens, and subsequently watched the\nblacks opening the body and making for the fat, but he became too sick and faintto observe anything further. With regard to people of maturer years, those who\nhave died suddenly and who are in good condition at the time of death — not the\nold or the emaciated — may similarly be eaten : this rarely takes place in the\nBoulia or Cloncurry Districts nowadays, though many of the older men of these\nparts will relate numerous instances of its occurrence in the \"early\" times. In\nthe Leichhardt-Selwyn District, the Kalkadoon at the present time (1896) will eat\nany corpse, friend or foe, old or young, even in cases where the flesh is visibly\nrotten with venereal . there is no doubt of this. Elsewhere individuals who have\nbeen killed in intertribal warfare are left exposed where they fall. At G-lenormiston, in 1892, on the occasion of a black having been killed by the tribe\ncollectively for murder, a great debate was held as to whether the body should be\neaten or not: it was only due to the presence upon the scene of the stationmanager (Mr. J. Coghlan, from whom I received the report) that decided the\nquestion in the negative. On the other hand, it is only fair to state that, so far\nas I have been able to gather information, I know of no case in North- West-\nCentral Queensland where any adult male or female has been killed for the\nsole purpose of providing a repast.\n\nrarooeo^^"

In the Leich hard t-Selwyn District. 298. Thunder and Lightningmaking.\n\n294. Rain-making : (a) In the Boulia District. — With the exception of perhaps\na few of the Tunda tribe, there are no individuals in the Boulia District who know\nhow to make rain. When rain is wanted here at Boulia, word is sent down to the\nMi orb' men at Springvale or the Diamantina Grates to come up and make some.\nThis special performance, carried out with a rain-stick (Fig. 408a.), a song, and\na dance, takes place somewhat as follows: — The rain-stick, koo-roo-mun-do, is\nformed of a thin piece of a species of \" white \" wood, about 20 iuches loDg,\non to the top of which is fixed a mass of the ordinary cementing-substance : into\nthis the three \"rain-stones,\" pieces of white quartz-crystal, are stuck. Hair cut\nfrom the beard is next laid lengthwise on to the cement, and fixed an inch or so\nbelow it : over this again are laid leafy branches of \" white \" wood which is all\ntied round with string, somewhat after the manner of a straw broom. Three\not four of such sticks may be used in the ceremony. At about mid-day, the men\nproceed to a secluded waterhole, one or more of their number having been\npreviously deputed to dive into the water and fix a hollowed log, about the length\nand thickness of a man's arm, vertically down into the mud. They now all get\ninto the water, and,\"surrounding the central individual, who holds the rain-stick, in\nmore or less of a circle, commence proceedings with a stamping movement of the\nfeet, each performer keeping the same relative position to the others : considering\nthat the water may be sometimes 4 or more feet in depth, the \" dancing \" is\nmaintained with no inconsiderable difficulty. During this part of the performance\nthe water is splashed with their hands, from all sides, onto the koo-roo-mun-do\nheld vertically on high by the central figure : there is a singing accompaniment\nto this, but the Pitta-Pitta men are evidently ignorant of its exact\nliteral purport. The singing over, the central figure dives out of sight,\nand attaches the rain -stick into the hollow log already fixed there : coming\nto the surface again he quickly climbs on to the bank, and spits out on dry\nland the water which while diving he had obtained from below. Should more\nthan one of these rain-sticks have been prepared, the performance is repeated\nwith each in turn. As they return to camp they now and again with a . small\ntwig, of any description, just scratch the tops of their heads -and the inner aspects\nof their shins, singing \"^wn-jo-pa-ripwn-jo-pa-ri \" (cf. Miorli pun-ja 9 the hair of\nthe head, sect. 52) in the former case, ana \" iodn-k$.-]}k-n \" in the latter (cf.\nKalkadoon wuritj-ka, the shin or leg, sect. 52) : it is believed that if the scratching\nwere to be done with the fingers direct, it would spoil the whole ceremony. On\nthe arrival of the party back at camp, the men who have been taking part in it\npaint themselves with gypsum in thick bands : from the top of the head down the\nmiddle of the face and neck as far as the umbilicus, a second transverse one over\nthe face across the bridge of the nose, and a third and fourth drawn from the\nextremities of the last-mentioned down the side of the neck over the shoulder\nalong the front and outer aspects of the arm and forearm to the wrist. During\nthe rest of the day, the scratching process, accompanied by the singing, is repeated\nat intervals, and the performance comes to a close. No woman is allowed to set\neyes on the raiD-stick or the ceremony of its submergence ; the wife of the\n\" boss\" rain-maker may, however, join in the subsequent twig-scratching. There\nwould appear to be no special individual among the Miorli who alone can make\nthe rain : any of the tribe can learn the process, and when once in possession of\none of these pieces of white quartz will be successful. When the rain does\neventually fall, the kooroomando is removed from out of the water. At Boulia,\nduring the heavy floods and rains of January and February, 1895, 1 was assured\n\n168 BAIff-MAKIXa, TIIUNDEB AND LIGHTNING-MAIOafG.\n\non native authority that all the rain and water had as usual been produced by the\nMiorli men : when I begged of them to immediately stay proceedings, the reply\ncame that as the flood had come up too quickly to allow of the removal of the\nrain-stick from out of its submerged position, the rain would have to run its\ncourse ! Instead of coming up to Boulia, the Miorli rain-makers may visit Marion\nDown's: from the former locality they may proceed for similar purposes to\nWarenda, Noranside, Chatsworth, &c."

All this time the women are\nencamped at from about 20 to 25 yards away. The men next form themselves\ninto a long string, Indian file, one behind the other, and gradually encircle the\ngins, over whom they throw the crushed and pulverised stone. A basis of white over the face,\nneck, arms, chest, and trunk down to the waist, with two parallel vertical bands of\nred passing down the centre. On the head is worn a thick roll of emu-feathers,\na sort of minma (sect. 286), with one wild-turkey feather stuck on top, to the\nshaft of which are attached five or six long opossum-string streamers falling down\nthe back. To the usual hair belt are fixed an eagle-hawk feather bundle (sect. 183)\nat either side, and one of white-cockatoo feathers in front. This rain-corrobboree\nwas \" found \" in these districts a very long time ago, and hence my informants\ncould render me no interpretation of the song accompanying the performance.\n\n297.   "passage_text": "THE ASHANTI CLASSIFICATORY SYSTEM 1

It is an axiom in anthropology that without a clear knowledge
of the family organization of a tribe it is impossible fully to
understand their social organizations. Therefore at the outset
of my investigations into the Anthropology of Ashanti, I
decided to give full consideration to this important question.

Before commencing the analysis of the data contained in
Tables I and II, a few brief explanatory notes will be given
touching the methods adopted by anthropologists for the elucidation of this problem. It will be seen that the chart is called
1 Ashanti Classificatory System ’. The term ‘ Classificatory ’ is
used in contradistinction to the term * Family ’ 2 (sometimes
called ‘ Descriptive ’). The latter is the term we would apply
to our own system of naming relatives. The essential basis of
the Classificatory System is that it is founded on the clan or
other social group larger than the family upon which our own
‘ descriptive ’ system is based.3

The next point to be touched upon is the method employed
in collecting the essential data, — data without which the results
of their system, so constantly present before our eyes but so
little understood, can never be fully grasped. This method is
known as the genealogical method.

This procedure, which was first successfully worked out by
the late Dr. Rivers, and has been elaborated by Mrs. Seligman,
is absolutely indispensable if any successful results are to be
obtained. Briefly the method consists in securing the services
of an elderly intelligent informant who is asked to give his

1 With pedigree chart.

2 See Kinship and Social Organization (Rivers).

3 It can of course be readily argued that our own Descriptive system is
in some degree classificatory, e. g. ' uncle ’ is applied to all brothers of father
or mother, while ‘ cousin ’ is used to denote an even wider circle. The word
Classificatory is used in these tables in a far wider sense. (We are all in
Ashanti familiar with the apparent confusion resulting from the indiscriminate
and unscientific use of the word ‘ brother which word need not necessarily
denote only a male child by the same father or mother as the speaker.)

genealogy.1 More than one genealogy should of course be taken
to avoid the possible chance of some double relationship : thus,
in table No. I, Kakari gave the relationship name for his father’s
sister’s husband as wofa, which stands for ‘ maternal uncle
but it was soon discovered that this was only because his uncle
had married the woman in question ; in the ordinary way the
man would be agya (father) ; this point is mentioned to show
one of many possible pitfalls.

Having secured the actual names of the individuals in the
family tree, it is not difficult to find out what relationship term,
with, in each case, its reciprocal, is used by them when speaking
of each other.

So much for a brief note of method ; for a fuller account
those interested should consult Notes and Queries on Anthropology, especially pp. 149-56, published by the Royal Anthropological Institute.

To come now to an analysis and examination of the
tables themselves. They contain a mass of details which have
bearing on :

1. Relationship Terms.

2. Clans, kinship or blood.

3. Descent.

4. Succession to Stools.

5. Inheritance of Property.

6. Marriages (Enjoined, Privileged, and Prohibited).

7. Ntoro, patrilineal exogamous divisions.

At the present stage of these investigations, which have so
far extended only over a comparatively short period, it is
obviously impossible to write exhaustively on any of these
subjects. In anthropology there is no single subject which the
student can take up and say, ‘ I am going to study this to
the exclusion of all else ’, for among primitive peoples there is
hardly an art, a rite, a custom, or belief that is not bound up
or connected in some way with some separate art, rite, custom,
or belief.

This chapter is therefore necessarily incomplete, and other

1 Pedigree Tables are illustrated in Man, April 1921, with an excellent
article on the methods, by Mrs. Seligman.

facts may appear later, which may alter or modify the conclusions arrived at. I nevertheless venture to present it in its
present form as I think it will show that, by the use of scientific
methods, the anthropologist is capable of throwing new light
in a comparatively short time on problems which have remained
obscure in these parts for over two centuries, and because I hope
that my account may stimulate further investigations by my
colleagues.

It may be as well here to recapitulate very briefly such
knowledge as we already possess on this subject."
}

  "passage_text": "THE ASHANTI CLASSIFICATORY SYSTEM

Each of these generations will now be examined in detail and
the points of especial importance noted. A mere list of relationship terms without an explanation of their meaning can only be
of minor value.

(A) It will be noted that ‘ in-laws ’ in this generation are
classed as akonta (sometimes heard akontagye), with one noticeable exception, i.e. the wife of a younger brother, who is called
by Kakari 'yere kuma (lit. small or secondary wife), with reciprocal
'kunu panyin, i.e. ‘ big or elder husband ’, and the reason for this
curious nomenclature will be clear later when, in the law of
inheritance, it comes to be noted that an elder brother, when
succeeding to a younger brother’s property on the latter’s
death, inherits his wife as forming part of the heritable property.
This potential marriage right gives him, even during his younger
brother’s life-time, the privilege of addressing his younger
brother’s wife as his ‘ younger wife ’. This, however, gives the
elder brother no right of access whatever during the husband’s
life-time.

Next it is to be noted that all the father’s brother’s sons
and daughters are called 'nua kuma,1 i.e. ‘ small or secondary
brothers ’, or agya 'ba, i.e. ‘ father’s child ’ ; ‘ father ’ here
referring, not to the speaker’s own father, but to his father’s
brothers, whom 1 A’ also calls ‘ father ’.

To an Ashanti the words agya ’ ba 2 (i.e. father’s child) implies
that a child of his father’s brother is meant ; and at once stamps
that child, if a female, as being in a prohibited degree of marriage
with the speaker for the reason to be given later when discussing
the ntoro relationship.

Dealing now with the spouses of these persons we have the
father’s brother’s son’s wife called 'yere kuma, i.e. ‘ small wife ’,
because her husband is called by ‘ A’ his, 1 A’s ’, ‘ small brother ’
(there is no right of access or marriage, however), or sometimes
akonta (i. e. sister-in-law). The father’s brother’s daughter’s

1 ’Nua kuma (i. e. younger or secondary brother or sister) is also used for
any of the following persons : (a) Own younger brother ; ( b ) own younger
sister ; (c) father’s sister’s son ; (d) mother’s sister’s son ; (e) mother’s
sister’s daughter ; (/) mother’s brother’s son. The females among all these, as
will be noted later, may not marry ‘A’.

2 Agya ’ba is used in an even wider sense implying the child of any man of
the speaker’s ntoro.

husband is also akonta. The mother’s sister’s son’s wife is called
by ‘A’ 'yere ( kuma ), i. e. ‘small wife’; because ‘A’ in certain
circumstances can claim her as his property on the death of her
husband. He has no right of access to her, however, during
her husband’s life-time. The mother’s sister’s daughter’s husband is akonta.

The sons and daughters (and their spouses) of ‘ A’s ’ father’s
sisters and ‘ A ’s’ mother’s brothers have terms (among others)
derived through their parents, i. e. the father’s sisters and
mother’s brothers. These paternal aunts and maternal uncles
have special terms due to the very especial position they hold,
while the father’s brothers and the mother’s sisters are all
indiscriminately classed as agya (father) and ena (mother)
respectively. The father’s sister’s son is called sewa ’ ba , i. e.
paternal aunt’s son, and the mother’s brother’s son is called
wofa 'ba, i. e. maternal uncle’s son. The father’s sister’s son is
also called agya wofase and 'nua kuma (small brother), with
reciprocal wafa 'ba (maternal uncle’s child), and also sometimes
akonta, i. e. brother-in-law.1

In referring to this alternative term akonta (brother-in-law)
given by ‘A’ to his father’s sister’s son, an interesting fact is
disclosed. We find that ‘A’ calls this man’s sister, i. e. his
father’s sister’s daughter, 'yere, i. e. ‘ wife ’. Now it will be found
on investigation that ‘ A’ has an absolute and undisputed right of
access to or marriage with this woman. So strong is this feeling
that ‘ A’ naturally calls her brother his akonta, i.e. brother-in-law,
though he may be only potentially so. An exactly similar
position exists on the mother’s side, where ‘A’ is the potential
husband and has right of access to (provided she is not, with
‘ A’s ’ permission, another man’s wife) the daughter of his
mother’s brother, whom ‘ A’ in consequence may call 'yere (wife),

1 It will be well here to draw attention to the almost universal misconception (due to that constant source of misinformation in West Africa, i. e.
the faulty rendering by interpreters whose knowledge of English is imperfect),
that ‘ uncle ’ or ' aunt ’ may equally refer to the maternal or paternal side ;
whereas in Ashanti the equivalents of our ‘ paternal uncle ’ and our ‘ maternal
aunt ’ do not exist ; and ' maternal aunts ’ and ‘ paternal uncles ’ are all
classed as ‘ mothers ’ and ‘ fathers ’. In contradistinction, certain relationships are singled out for distinct and separate names because of their
importance in the family organization, this being a normal feature of the
classificatory system.

3i
with reciprocal 'kunu (husband), at the same time calling her
brother akonta, i.e. brother-in-law.1 Both these marriages are
called Cross-Cousin Marriages.

Next we come to the wives of the father’s sister’s son and the
mother’s brother’s son ; both are called by 1 A’ 'yere kuma (small
or secondary wife), or sometimes akonta. The reason ‘A’ calls
these women his ‘ small wives ’ is that the husband in each case
stands to ‘A’ in the relationship of ’ nua , i. e. brother, hence, as
in the case of ‘ A’s ’ younger brothers, he calls their wives his
wives ; the name in these cases, however, being only a sort of
courtesy title and implying (at the present date at any rate) no
rights over them."

  "passage_text": "(B) First generation of ‘ A’s ’ ascendants. It has already
been noted that all ‘ A’s ’ father’s brothers are called by
‘A’ agya (father), and all his mother’s sisters are called ena
(mother), while his father’s sisters are called by the special
name sewa, and the mother’s brothers by the special name
wofa ; reciprocals respectively 'ba (child) and wofase (sister’s
child).

‘ A’s ’ mother’s brother’s wife is called ase ; now ase is used
of ‘ in-laws ’ (fathers, mothers, &c.), and its use here would appear
extraordinary, had it not already been pointed out that ‘ A’ has
the right of access to and marriage with his mother’s brother’s
daughter ; hence his mother’s brother’s wife is his potential
mother-in-law and the terminology at once becomes logical and
the meaning clear. The mother’s sister’s husband and the
father’s sister’s husband are agya , reciprocal 'ba. The father’s
brother’s wife is ena , reciprocal 'ba.

(C) Generation iii) of ascendants. All are classed, without
exception, as nana.

(D) First generation of ‘ A’s ’ descendants. All the sons- and
daughters-in-law are ase, with reciprocal ase. The brother’s sons
and brother’s daughters are all classed as 'nua mma, i.e. simply
brother’s children. The brother’s son’s wives and the brother’s
daughter’s husbands are all ase, as are the sister’s son’s wives.
When we come ta the sister’s sons, however, we again have the

1 If ‘A’ does not marry these women but permits them to marry some one
else, he then has the right to marry their daughters whom he will call from
birth me yere (my wife), and the mother who was first of all his potential
wife becomes his potential mother-in-law and is actually so called, i. e. ase.

823149

C

important and distinct terms, i. e. wofase, with reciprocal wofa —
when the man is speaking ; when a woman is speaking the
sister’s son is simply 'ba (child).

Coming to the mother’s sister’s children’s children, and the
mother’s brother’s children’s children (not shown on the chart),
we find that the mother’s sister’s daughter’s sons and daughters
are called by 1 A’ wofase , with reciprocal wofa , and their spouses
are called ase. The mother’s sister’s son’s children and the
mother’s brother’s son’s children are to ‘A’ simply mma (sing.
'ba), i. e. his children, and they call ‘A’ agya, father (adding
name, e. g. Kakari).

When we come to the children of the mother’s brother’s
daughter we have apparently a most baffling and complicated
terminology, for we are told by one that of these, the daughter
is called by ‘A’ 'yere (wife), with reciprocal 'kunu (husband) ;
by another that ‘A’ would call this woman me ’ ba (my child) ;
and by a third that she would stand to 1 A’ in the relationship
of wofase (sister’s daughter).

What complicates the matter still more is that the inquirer
will find that in actual practice one and all of these relationships
will be found to exist in different families, and he will be informed
in each case it is the normal and proper relationship according
to the native customary law.

The son of 1 A’s ’ mother’s brother’s daughter we also will
find stated may stand to ‘ A’ either in the relationship of actual
‘ son ’, or that of wofase (sister’s son). This is the kind of
problem that causes the casual inquirer to despair, or go away
believing that no order or settled design underlies native institutions, which he will suppose are subject to mere caprice, instead
of, as is really the case, being ordained by rigid and well-defined
laws, which fit one into another in the social organization and
seldom seem to clash.

The following explanation will, I trust, make the matter
clearer. The mother’s brother’s daughter’s children may, we
found, stand in any of the following relations to ‘A’, i. e. they
may be :

(a) His own children.

(b) (In case of a daughter) his wife.

(c) His wofase (i.e. his sister’s sons).

(a) ‘ A’s ’ own children : we have seen that 1 A’ has an undisputed right of access to and marriage with his mother’s brother’s
daughter. If, then, he marries this woman her children will be
his children, hence those who state that this relationship exists
between ‘A’ and the potential children of a mother’s brother’s
daughter are stating a fact which is based on native custom.

(b) Again, we have seen that should ‘A’ not exercise his
privilege to marry his mother’s brother’s daughter, he will then
still have the right to marry her daughter ; if he does so, she
then becomes his wife.

(c) Supposing again that ‘A’, by agreement, gives up his
prior right to this daughter of his mother’s brother’s daughter,
as he did already to her mother, she, i. e. the mother’s brother’s
daughter’s daughter becomes known by ‘A’ as his wofase, i. e.
‘sister’s child’, because her mother is now called by ‘A’ his
’nua, ‘ sister ’.

A universally-known Ashanti saying, which runs, ‘ Se w'anya
wo wo fa 'ba ana wose wofase anware a, wo ’ nua ne no' (‘ If you
did not get your mother’s brother’s child or your father’s sister’s
child to marry, she is your own sister ’), shows the whole aspect
of the case as viewed by an Ashanti.

The above also explain the double terminology given for the
mother’s brother’s daughter’s son, who may be ‘ A’s ’ own child
or his wofase, i. e. sister’s child.

It must be clearly understood that the courtesy title of wofase
in this case implies no ‘blood’ tie with ‘A’, and is really a
fictitious relationship carrying with it none of the privileges of
the blood-related wofase as to succession to property and stool.1

Everything that has been written above concerning the
mother’s brother’s daughter’s daughter applies with equal force
to the father’s sister’s daughter’s daughter, who may be ‘ A’s ’
‘ own child ’, ‘ own wife ’, or ‘ sister’s child ’, i. e. wofase.

The children of ‘ A’s ’ father’s brother’s children’s children are
all mma (children), reciprocal agya (father)."
}

  "passage_text": "(E) Second generation of ‘ A’s ’ descendants. All the persons
in this generation are classed as nana and their spouses ase
(in-laws).

1 This point might be of great importance in stool or succession cases and
should be carefully noted.

(F) Third generation of ‘ A’s ’ descendants. Here we have
again an instructive term. All the persons in this generation
are classed as nana n'ka'so, i. e. ‘ grandchild (&c.), don’t touch
(my) ear with reciprocal nana panyin (old grandfather). The
significance of this term will be dealt with later under the heading
of Prohibited Marriages.

Table II (Wife's pedigree). In this table, which is incomplete,
several points of interest should be noted.

The wife’s sister is called by ‘ A’ 'yere (wife). This, as far as
I can discover, does not (now) imply any right of access or
marriage. In this connexion, however, it is of importance to
note that in the case of chiefs, when a wife dies, the wife’s family
are expected to replace the deceased woman by giving her sister
in marriage to the chief. Some potential right to a wife’s sister
in the past is further postulated by the name given to a wife’s
sister’s husband; he is called by ‘A’ kora (reciprocal kora).
Now kora is the word used also for a co-wife, and means literally
‘ the jealoua one h1 Again we find that this woman’s children
(i. e. the wife’s sister’s children) are called by ‘A’ ‘ my wife’s
children ’.

These facts are, I think, particularly suggestive.

The wife’s brother’s daughter is called akonta 'ba, i. e. brotherin-law’s child, but there is an alternative title, ase, which here
means ‘ daughter-in-law ’, and the reason given for this name
is that one of ‘ A’s ’ sons 1 will probably marry this woman
The whole question of ‘ arranged ’ marriages appears to me to
be worthy of very close investigation.

This completes the ‘ relationships system ’ proper. Its classificatory character can be seen very clearly. In itself such a list
is of considerable value and interest, but passing on to its
application, its importance in getting anything like a full grasp
of Ashanti social organizations, will come even more fully to
be realized.

2. Clans ( Abusua ). It was already known that the Ashanti
were divided into exogamous clans. Bowdich noted this fact
more than a hundred years ago, while Christaller writes : ‘ The
principle of the division into families is descendance from the

1 Mrs. Seligman tells me that among some of the Nilotic tribes the word for
co-wife is also derived from a root meaning jealous.

same mother, or relation from the mother’s side, which relation
also determines the right of inheritance among the genuine Tshi
Tribes.’ 1 Bosman, writing in 1700, also notes the same system.

It is not intended, in this chapter, to enter into a full account
of these clans, their number, names, origin, &c. They are only
dealt with here in relation to their bearing on the subject under
discussion.

In Table I of the chart, seven clans are dealt with, all of which
are actually the clans of the persons named in that genealogy.

The first important rule to note is that these clans ( abusua )
are exogamous, that is, a person of one clan can under no possible
circumstances marry or have sexual intercourse with any one
who belongs to his or her clan. Infringement of this law was
punished by death, or expulsion from the clan, for both parties
concerned.2

The second is that descent is matrilineal, i. e. a man or woman
belongs to the clan not of the father but of the mother. These
clans are, in the chart, shown by distinctive patterns, which
indicate at a glance how the clan persists as long as the direct
female descendants last, but is immediately lost in the children
of any male. This fact is the very basis of the Ashanti social
organization, and once fully grasped and understood, explains
most of their laws of inheritance, succession, and marriage, and
accounts for the strangeness of these rules and of their relationship terminologies.

The Ashanti word for clan is abusua , and this word is
synonymous with mogya (blood). There is a well-known proverb
which runs Abusua bako mogya bako, ‘ one clan one blood ’.

Bowdich wrote : ‘ This extraordinary rule of succession excluding all children but those of a sister is founded on the
argument that if the wives of the sons are faithless the blood of
the family is entirely lost in the offspring, but should the
daughters deceive their husbands it is still preserved.’

A glance at the chart will show the complete fallacy of any
such argument and prove how totally this subject' has been
misunderstood. Take a couple, say Kakari and his wife, Ya

1 Vide also Sarbah, Fanti Customary Laws, pp. 3-5.

2 Expulsion from the clan amounted to outlawry and was a very solemn
proceeding.

Gyansua ; the former is of the Ekuona clan, the latter (the
woman) of the Beretuo clan. They have a child, i. e. son Kojo
Nti, who is, according to Ashanti idea, of the mother’s clan
(Beretuo), i. e. he has his mother’s blood. This we will suppose,
for the sake of the argument, is the blood it is wished to preserve. This son now marries, but he is, by customary law,
compelled to marry some one of a clan other than Beretuo.
He marries a woman of the Asokore clan. Now, however
virtuous his wife may be or if she be a hundred times unfaithful,
matters not at all so far as keeping the Beretuo blood pure is
concerned, for the woman’s offspring can never be of the Beretuo
clan ; but if she married twenty men of every possible clan and
bore twenty children, all would be her own blood, i. e. Asokore ;
because the men cannot transmit one drop of their blood to
their children ; on the other hand, a Beretuo woman would
transmit her blood to her children, to be lost entirely in her
son’s offspring, to continue however in the female side, i. e. her
daughter’s granddaughters, &c., as long as the female line
lasted."
}
